subtopic: MOTION FOE APPLICATION OF HULE 17B ON SECOND READING OF BILL
speechtext:
This Bill if passed will not do me any harm.
I stand to gain by it. The proposal to enfranchise the female relatives of the soldiers will probably increase my majority by a considerable amount. I have no alien citizens in my constituency, but there are Conservatives there who are fair-minded and who like to see fair play, and, if I judge them rightly, they will resent this measure. It is not giving away any secret to say that that is the feeling generally on this side of the House. We on this side of the Chamber feel that, in the step that is being taken now, the Government have over-reached themselves. There is a feeling in this country that a man should take a .fighting chance. He takes it in western Canada, and, he takes it in eastern Canada. Among the school boys in the province
from which I come the desire for fair play is almost a passion, and there is always a feeling of contempt for the man who takes a mean advantage, the man who hits below the belt.
The danger of this measure is that it lends itself to fraud. While our party stand to gain in some particulars, we stand to lose in others. The administration of this measure in some cases, no doubt, will fall into the hands of dishonest officials. The provisions of the Bill, so far as I have been able to learn, are complicated and intricate. Permit me to make a proposal, Mr. Speaker, that you should scrutinize this Bill from first to last and give me your honest opinion about it. I confess when I read it, and when I discovered the complicated provisions relating to the tied ballot which has been abandoned in western Canada, I believe, for some years, because it was notorious for the frauds brought about under it. When I saw the extraordinary power that was given to irresponsible local enumerators, and tl\e provisions relating to the soldiers' grandfathers and the Syrian Christians, I felt in my own mind: for God's sake, what kind of franchise are we going to have in this country if the Secretary of State (Mr. Meighen) continues to tamper With it, twist it and bedevil it, as he has been doing for the last two or three weeks. It reminds me, Mr. Speaker, of the German buccaneers in Southwest Africa, whose plan was to fight the British forces in the present war by poisoning all the wells. The title of the Bill is "The War-Times Elections Act." Let me suggest to the Secretary of State that he change the name, and call it "The War-Times Prussian Jun-!<er Act." The idea behind this measure is military autocracy. We, oft this side of the House, I am proud to say, stand for democracy. If hon. gentlemen opposite want autocracy, why go to all this trouble to get it. They can get it without resorting to such a measure as this. All they have to do is to hold up their hands, lay down their arms, and the Kaiser will give it to them. Military autocracy is the same wherever you find it. British military rule or Canadian military rule is not one whit better in its aim than German military rule.

subtopic: MOTION FOE APPLICATION OF HULE 17B ON SECOND READING OF BILL
speechtext:
We had it in .Scotland in the days of the "big killing/' when my countrymen and the countrymen of other gentlemen in this House were shot like wild beasts in the glens and hills because they insisted on their right to worship God according to the dictates of their own conscience. Thank God these days are past in the old land, and they are also past here, and, notwithstanding the puny efforts of hon. gentlemen opposite, they will never return. But it becomes necessary for ue. at this late date, 1917, to reassert the doctrine that every man has a right to have a say in the election of the representatives of the people; to have a voice in the determination of who shall govern the country in which he lives.
This Bill contains three main provisions. First, it disfranchises about a million women who live between the Ottawa river and the Pacific coast. The women of these five provinces are now entitled to vote. That is in direct violation of a resolution of this -House, moved by the Prime Minister; it is in direct violation of what every man in this House and in this country understood to be the pledge of the Prime Minister. Why was it done, Mr. Speaker? It would not have been done if the Government could profit by abstaining from it. This Government have scoured the world for votes; they have given votes to men who never saw Canada, who never set foot in Canada, and probably never will. The only explanation of their conduct in dis- [DOT] franchising the women of Canada in these five provinces is that they believe they will vote against the Government. I do not need to refer to the self-denial and fortitude of the women of Canada and the way that they have helped to carry on this war. I do not need to say that the women of Canada deserve better treatment at the hands of this Government.
The second provision of the Bill enfranchises the female relations of soldiers, both East and West. I heartily agree with that provision of the Bill. The only objection that can be made to that provision is that it is class legislation; it is not fair to those who have been left out, practically all of whom have made great sacrifices for the cause for which we all stand.
The third provision of the Bill is the most important one; it disfranchises men of alien birth. I submit that this provision is a vicious one; it is a breach of faith on the part of the Government of this country. We invited these people from northern Europe to come to Canada. We

promised them land; we promised them the rights of citizenship; we promised them protection under the flag. We boasted that we had such a thing in this country as British fair play. We assured them that Canada was the home of liberty and the refuge of the oppressed from every land. They took us at our word-and what are we doing now? We are branding them as outlaws and as perjured traitors. After three years residence and good behaviour, they came forward to take the oath of allegiance in order that they might become naturalized British subjects. Thi- is what they promised:
I do sincerely promise and swear that I will be faithful and bear true allegiance to His Majesty King George V as lawful sovereign of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and of the Dominion of Canada, dependent on and belonging to said kingdom, and that I will defend him to the utmost of my power against all traitorous conspiracies or attempts whatsoever which shall be made against his person, crown and dignity, and that I will do my utmost endeavours to disclose and make known to His Majesty, his heirs or successors, all treasons or traitorous conspiracies or attempts which I shall know to be against him or any of them, and all this I do swear without any equivocation, mental evasion or secret reservation. So help me, God.
They took that oath, and we have the testimony of hon. gentlemen who have lived among them that they have kept it faithfully. We are now preparing to break our promise to them,-and in doing so we put ourselves in the same position as that taken by the German Kaiser. What will President Wilson say about this action on the part of the Canadian Government? He has sent out a clear call to the young men of the United States. He has taken high ground; he has summoned half a million men to the colours. What for? To establish the great principle that every free man has the right to help select the government under which he is to live. He refuses even to negotiate with a government that does not hold, office by the voice of the people.
I object to this measure, first, because it is designed to serve party and not public ends; second, because it is despotic and unjust in so far as the disfranchisement is concerned. If the Government of this country, assisted by closure and backed up by a political machine called the Senate, can disfranchise one class of the people, what is to prevent them from taking a like step in regard to any other class that is suspected of being hostile to the Government? Why not, Sir, disfranchise every maS who joins a labour union in this country? There is no reason why the Government should

not do that. That is what is in their hearts and minds; they only lack the courage to do it. They have not done it because they dare not do it. Do the gentlemen composing -this moribund Government think that the Galicians and the Moravians have no friends? Let me say to hon. gentlemen opposite that the hatred of tyranny is in the 'heart of every free man, and, once kindled, it has to be reckoned with. It was to vindicate this principle that we fought the South African war.
Going back to the history of that event, you will find that British intervention was justified on one ground, and on one ground alone. That ground was that British settlers in South Africa were not allowed to have a say in the election of representatives of the people. President Paul Kruger, in 1899, did what our modern-*

-Paul Kruger of Portage la Prairie is attempting to do in 1917. Kruger denied to British subjects in South. Africa the right to vote until they had been in the country a period of twelve years. In the year 1899 he introduced the Transvaal Franchise Act, which was on all fours with this measure. You would suppose from reading this Bill that the Secretary of State had obtained his inspiration from Kruger's Franchise Act; The only difference is that this Bill is more oppressive. Kruger required a residence of twelve years; this Bill requires a residence of fifteen years-indeed, eighteen years, because a man has to be three years in the country before he can take the oath of allegiance. The Transvaal Franchise Act denied to all citizens who were not burghers or Boers the right to vote. The enfranchised Englishmen, or TJitlander, as he was called, could become a burgher after twelve years' residence. The Government of Great Britain protested against this long period of probation. The Uitlanders themselves protested. There was great excitement in the Transvaal, in the Cape and in England. Great indignation was expressed at the injustice that had been perpetrated. Large meetings were held in the mining districts of South Africa; an immense delegation was appointed to wait on President Kruger. They put forward every possible argument; They appealed to him as a Christian and as a sf&tesman and as a man. But he was immovable. The London Times published . at the time the short, defiant speech that Kruger made on that occasion in reply to the delegation. It was as follows:
Burghers, friends, thieves, murderers, newcomers, and others:	Go back and tell your
people that I shall never give them anything.
I shall never change my policy; now let the storm burst.

speechtext: What does the Kruger from Manitoba say?

subtopic: MOTION FOE APPLICATION OF HULE 17B ON SECOND READING OF BILL
speechtext:
I am glad to say that the burghers were not all of one mind. A party in South Africa led by Joubert stood for moderation and fair play. In an eloquent speech, he opposed the Franchise measure.
He said:
If you pass this you might as well obliterate from the arms of the republic the motto that unity makes strength.
But Kruger had his way; the law passed; the storm burst, and it broke against the shores of Canada- My right hon. leader who was at that time the Prime Minister of this country sent out a call to. the young men of Canada, and 8,000 of them answered the call -and went to that distant part of the Empire to fight for the flag. Some of them never came back. At Paardeburg, the Modder river and other places on the lonely veldt of South Africa you will today see little wooden crosses marking the graves of some 200 Canadians who perished in that struggle. They gave their lives in defence of the' principles for which we stand here to-day. Did they throw away their lives? Will any man say that those men died in vain? I make the statement, Mr. Speaker, without fear of successful contradiction, that this Bill is a direct insult to their memories. This House of Commons at that time, by a solemn resolution, unanimously condemned in anticipation the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite- This -resolution, which w-as moved by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, seconded by Mr. Foster and unanimously adopted, read:
1.	Resolved, that this House has viewed with regret the complications which have arisen in the Transvaal Republic, of which Her Majesty is suzerain, from the refusal to accord to Her Majesty's subjects now settled in that region, any adequate participation in its government;
2.	Resolved, that this House has learned with still greater regret that the condition of things there existing has resulted in intolerable oppression, and has produced great and dangerous excitement among several classes of Her Majesty's subjects in her South African possessions;
3.	Resolved, that this House, representing a people which has largely succeeded, by the adoption of the principle of conceding equal political rights to every portion of the population, in harmonizing estrangements and in producing general content with the existing system of government, desires to express its sympathy with the efforts of Her Majesty's Imperial authorities to obtain for the subjects of

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to occupy more than -a very few minutes in regard to the question now before the House. This matter divides itself into two parts, namely, the giving of the franchise to certain women in the country and the disfranchising of certain men in the country. I do not agree with the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) when he says that this Bin disfranchises one million women in this country. We cannot disfranchise those- who do not possess the franchise. We cannot take away from them that which they do not possess. Therefore, I say that his remark in that regard is entirely erroneous. The hon. gentleman saw fit to draw attention in his remarks to the fact that the vote was being given to certain men who, he said uever lived in Canada and perhaps never will live in Canada. In that, he referred to those British subjects, who, living in the United States, saw fit to don the uniform and go overseas to fight in this great war in our behalf. I think the hon. gentleman's opposition to the extension of the franchise to those men will not be received with acclaim by many people in this country. Even in his own constituency, I doubt very

much if lie will find many to agree with him in his opposition to the granting of the franchise to those brave men who have gone overseas to do for us what a number of people in this country have shown no disposition to do for themselves. The hon. gentleman has referred to Krugerism, Kaiserism, Prussianism and the Boer war. He was very strong in his expression of disapproval of Krugerism. Might I remind the hon. member that his attitude to-day is somewhat different from the attitude of his party at the time Kruger defied Britain in South Africa? The attitude of his party at that time was one of standing still until the sentiment of this country forced them to take action, and it was only under that compulsion that they sent some troops to South Africa to put down Krugerism, and even then they sent them on the C.O.I). principle. The hon. gentleman says that the men who gave their lives in South Africa died for principles for which they on that side of the House stand. He might have added to that that they died for the principles for which we on this side of the House move. That is the distinction between the two parties: They "stand" and we "move." They stood in the matter of the war in South Africa until the people made them move. They have stood in the matter of this war; and so far as they are concerned, if we are to judge from their present attitude, there would have been very few Canadians overseas, had hon. gentlemen opposite been in power in this country instead of the party which is in power.
As to the granting of votes to women, might I remind hon. gentlemen opposite of what took place in this House away back in 1895, when Mr. Davin, then member for Assiniboia, moved, on the 8th of May:
That in the opinion of this House, the privilege of voting for candidates for membership thereof should be extended to women possessing the qualifications which now entitle men to the electoral franchise.
That motion was opposed by the right hon. gentleman who now leads the Opposition, who moved in amendment that:
The question of woman suffrage is one which, like other questions concerning the suffrage, more properly belongs to provincial jurisdiction.
In other words, he shifted the whole responsibility to the provinces, and raised the issue whether there should be a provincial or Dominion franchise for Federal purposes. In the course of his remarks on that occasion, he said that so far as the province of Quebec was concerned, there

was no sentiment in favour of granting the franchise to women; the sentiment, on the contrary, was just the other way. He said:
I am not sure that the granting of the franchise to women would be altogether an unmixed evil. I am not sure that it would tend to the harmony or to the improvement of domestic life which after all is the proper centre of woman's influence. ... Whether the suffrage is applied to women or to any other class, it is largely a question of education, largely a question of social disposition, largely a question of habit. Let the provinces decide the question. There may be provinces where from the education of the people, from their social habits, it might be conducive to the general good of the country that women should be admitted to the franchise. As to the province from which I come, I must say that it is not prepared for woman suffrage. .	.	.
'f the proposition were made in the local Legislature of Quebec to confer the suffrage on women, I am quite sure it would be voted down at once. Speaking for the province of Quebec, I am certainly right in saying that women do not feel it an injustice that they have no right to vote on any political question.
If, therefore, this Bill went the length the hon. member for Guysborough says it should go, and granted the franchise to all women, it would be disapproved of more heartily by the right hon. gentleman who now leads the Opposition than if it granted only a partial franchise to women. In other words, if all the women of the province of Quebec and other provinces were to be enfranchised, instead of only some of them, as under this Bill, the grievance of that province, if it is a grievance at all, would certainly be much greater.
This measure proposes to give to certain women in this country a voice in the selecting of the next Government of this Dominion. Why should the franchise be extended to these particular women, rather than to all women in this country? Will any person say that the women who have worked for the Red Cross and other patriotic societies, making comforts for the soldiers, should be put on the same footing, even though some of them have worked night and day almost, with the women whose relatives are overseas? I believe there will be no outcry from these women themselves, because their sisters whose relatives are overseas are to be given the right to vote.
But there is another reason why these women whose husbands and sons and brothers are overseas should be selected for this honour on this occasion. They have an especial interest in the selecting of the next Government which will control the destinies of this country for the next four or five years. They have an especial in-

terest in seeing that the honour their men have won for this country is not put to shame by a Government which would be controlled by the anti-British and foreign element in this Dominion. That, I say, is their right on this occasion. What injustice is being done to the foreign element, the alien enemies in this country, in excluding them from the franchise? One can understand that men of Austrian or German birth might feel very diffident about enlisting and going to the front, possibly to fight against their own cousins and brothers in this great struggle. But if these men of alien enemy birth are not prepared to assume their full share of responsibility as citizens of this country, they certainly should not ask for all the privileges that go with citizenship in this country. Citizenship is not a one-sided affair. It grants certain privileges to a man, but it also entails the assumption of certain responsibilities, and it seems to me that in view of the struggle that is going on in Europe at the present time, no injustice is being done to those men who have so far shown little or no disposition to take part in that great struggle, by excluding them from the franchise. What right have men to call out in the name of liberty, who have made no effort to maintain that liberty? What right have men to call out in the name of democracy and democratic government who are not prepared to fight to maintain democratic government and democratic principles? What injustice is being done to any man who has shown no disposition to uphold the principles of democracy on which the government of this country is founded, by refusing him a say in the election of a government in this democratic country?
The next election will be entirely different from any other election ever held in this country. There will be no fiscal issue before the people. The only issue will be: Shall we place in power in the Dominion of Canada for the next four or five years a government that is in sympathy with British institutions and prepared to keep faith with the boys who have gone overseas, or a government chosen from a party who have shown by their conduct that they are not in sympathy with British institutions, and that they are not prepared to keep faith with the boys overseas and back them up with the reserves that are required? That is the question for the people of Canada to decide in the next election. It will not be a question of tariff or of fiscal policy. The

question will be: Shall this country be controlled for the next four or five years by men who are in sympathy with British institutions and democratic principles and prepared to do their part in maintaining them, or shall it he controlled by men backed up by the anti-British and foreign element in this country who so far have shown, not only no disposition to maintain the principles which hon. gentlemen opposite so loudly acclaim in this Chamber, but in many cases have shown a disposition to block all progress along the line pt maintaining those principles as they should be maintained, and a disposition not to back up our men ait the front. Therefore, for these reason, I give my hearty support to this measure.
Right Hon, Sir WILFRED LA DRIER: Mr. Speaker, in all federated countries it was for a long time a much discussed question as to what power should regulate the franchise. Two ideas were advanced, one that the franchise should be regulated by each legislative body, whether it w*as the local body or the central body. The other that there should be only one franchise, as there was only one country to be represented, and what division there was, was not in the people but in the nature of the power which was entrusted either to the local body or to the central body. After long discussion, the prevailing idea was that there should be only one franchise, and that whether the people were represented in the local legislatures or in the central Parliament it should be only the same electorate that should act. The American constitution, indeed, on this point is very definite. The second article reads:
The House of Representatives shall be composed of members chosen every second year by the people of the several states, and the electors in each state shall have the qualifications requisite for electors of the most numerous branch of the State Legislature.
So, in the United States, the franchise is regulated by each of the 45 States of the Union. There is no franchise for Congress, but the members of the Congress are elected by this franchise which exists in the several states of the Union. Our Constitution did not go that far, but it provided, by article 41, that until the Parliament of Canada had otherwise legislated, the franchise as it existed in the year 1867 in each one of the provinces, should be the franchise upon which the House of Commons would be elected. That state of thing continued until the year 1885,
4 p.m. when this Parliament enacted a franchise for itself, which fran-

chise existed until the year 1897; and I ask the judgment of every man in this House, either on this side or on the other side, as to whether the Dominion franchise which existed from 1885 to 1897 ever gave the same satisfaction as the provincial franchises had given before the year 1885. From the year 1897 up to the present time, the franchise for this Federal House has been the provincial franchise, and I think I may say, again placing myself under the judgment of every man in this House, that the provincial franchise has given full satisfaction.
If I understood aright the speech delivered by the Secretary of State the other day, when he moved the second reading of this Bill-and I think I did understand it aright -he rather agreed with the principle of maintaining the provincial franchises for election to this House of Commons. But though he agreed in principle that the members of this House should be elected under the franchises in each province, he proceeded to stab the provincial franchises in three particulars.
In the first place the franchise which exists in the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and British Columbia, make no distinction at all between class and class-it gives the franchise to every British subject. My hon. friend by this Bill, however, provides that an important class of His Majesty's subjects shall be denied the privilege which they are now enjoying in each of those provinces.

speechtext:
If my hon.
friend will permit me I will say: that is
very specious reasoning. Chinese and Japanese are not voters., but the Germans and Austrians are voters, and they have been voters from the time they were naturalized. The object of my hon. friend is to take away from these men of foreign origin the rights and privileges of British subjects, which have been freely granted to them by the provinces I have mentioned-
That is what I blame my hon. friend for to-day. He is introducing a new principle and violating the franchise granted by his own province of Manitoba to these men. And, for what reason? Because, forsooth, they are of foreign origin. Because they may have been born in Germany, or Austria, or Turkey, they -are. not supposed to be able to give an unbiased verdict upon the questions before the country. Well, for my part, and I speak frankly, I do not admit that doctrine. I do not admit the doctrine that when a man leaves Europe- whatever may be the part of Europe whence he comes

and comes to this country, when he swears allegiance to His Majesty the King, when he becomes a citizen of Canada, when he builds a home for himself and for his family, I am not prepared to believe that if a conflict arises between the land of that man's birth and the land of his adoption, that he will go back upon the country to which he as sworn allegiance.
I can well believe that if there be men of German origin who have forsaken Germany and who have become British subjects in -this country-having made their homes here and established their families here-that they may be suffering agony at this time, but I am not prepared to believe that they will turn traitor to the land of their adoption in favour of the land of their birth. They have given up the land of their birth because conditions were not satisfactory to them, because they were living under tyranny, because their Government would not respect its pledges; and they came to a land which they were taught and were told would hold sacred whatever promises or pledges it made to them. If you tell me that in a conflict between Germany and Great Britain these men will turn traitor to the land in which they have enjoyed freedom and happiness, . I am not prepared to believe it. There may be cases here and there of men who will do so, but that the great mass of such people would, is something I do not believe. The men who came to Canada from Germany are very few. The great bulk of immigration did not come from the Empire of Germany. There are some German settles in the

Galicians, Bukowinians, and Rumanians, that these different races will be disposed to come to this country, when they know that Canada has not kept its pledges and promises to the people from foreign countries who have settled in our midst, and when they know that in the United States there was never any attempt to curtail or interfere with the rights as American citizens which immigrants to that country were granted. It seems to me that in this condition of things there is a thought which will make Parliament pause before proceeding further with this Bill. This is not a Liberal measure, it is not a Canadian measure, and it is not a British measure. It is a retrograde measure and a German measure. The position taken by the Government cannot be justified. If you want to have the true intent and meaning of this Bill, you must go beyond the Bill itself, because within the four corners of the Bill there is no justification which could induce any man on the other side of the House to vote for if For my paTt I hope that it is not too late to ask Parliament to pause, and to consider the -bad precedent which it is establishing, which must be far-reaching in its consequences. I ask my hon. friend to reflect, upon this. The measure is such that it must have serious consequence. If it be said in Canada that the pledges which we have given to immigrants when inviting them to come to this country to settle with us, can be broken with impunity, that we will not trust these men, and that we will not be true to the promises which we made to them,, then I despair of the future of this country. I could not expect that in future we shall have the same measure of satisfaction that we have had in the past in our efforts to induce immigration, if we follow such a principle.
I again call to the attention of my hon. friends on the other side the comparison which will be made between the treatment which is accorded to immigrants in the United States, and the treatment which is accorded them by the Canadian authorities. Look at the action of the American Congress, when that country came into the war. The Congress made more preparatipn for war in six months than we did perhaps, in three years. They looked over the whole field and covered it, but they never thought of disfranchising anybody, even when the country was overrun by German spies, when German spies were engaged in treachery and trickery, when they were trying to dislocate even the production of munitions. When such were to

be found everywhere and anywhere, the American Congress did not, for a single moment, think of depriving the. German settler of the rights and privileges which he had received as an American citizen. Is that not the course which we ourselves should pursue? Should we not follow the example of the United States in this regard, rather than introduce legislation of such a retrograde character as this?
I am sorry to have to take the position which I have taken on this point. I have been supporting the Government on the war policy up to the present session. I am sorry that the occasion arose during this session when I had to discontinue my support of the Government on a measure of great importance. I am sorry that I have to again dissent with the Government on this measure. But I believe-and we shall all be judged some day by our actions here-that in this instance the Government is taking a step which will cause serious injury to the country, and, therefore, Sir, actuated by these sentiments I beg to move:
That this Bill be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that the abridgment by this Parliament of the electoral franchise now enjoyed in any province of the Dominion by any class of His Majesty's subjects would be contrary to the peace, order, and 'good government of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, in the limited time at my disposal I shall not be able to follow my right hon. ..friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) in all that he has said. It may, however, be worth while to point out that he is seriously astray in some of his assertions. ' It is not true, although he asserted that it was, that all naturalized British subjects in the four western provinces have the right to vote; that can be demonstrated to him by the production of the provincial statutes bearing upon the question. He seemed to be under the impression, also, that women who have gone overseas as nurses with the Canadian Expeditionary Forces have not the right to vote. He emphasized this by declaring that in some cases they have been under fire. I beg to assure him that all members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, whether men or women, have the right to vote at the forthcoming election. Not only is that the case, but, as I am reminded by the Secretary of State (Hon. Arthur Meighen), the female relatives in this country of such women also have the right to vote at the- election to be held in the early future.
My right hon. friend has taken issue with the opinion of the law officers of the Crown

as to the construction of the Dominion Elections Act. He asserts that all women on the provincial lists have the right to vote at Dominion elections. I can only say to him that the Minister of Justice (Hon. C. J Doherty), the Solicitor General, and all the legal authorities whom the Government consulted on this question, entertain an opinion directly opposite to that for which my right hon. friend stands sponsor. He will realize that under the circumstances wo are bound to take the opinion of the law officers of the Crown, and of other eminent legal authorities to whom I have alluded, rather than his own.
My right hon. friend has called to his aid the example of the United States. No federal election has been held in the United States since that country became a belligerent; therefore he has nothing to offer to us from the example of the United .States. Nor can he offer anything to us from the example of the United States until he is able to point to their action under conditions similar to those which confront this country at present. He omitted altogether in his statement any reference to the well known fact that Australia has given us an example of legislation of precisely the same character as this, except that here we have not gone as far as Australia has.
My right hon. friend has seen fit, for what reason I do not know, to disparage this country by stating that the United States have done more in four or five months-I suppose he meant proportionately-than this country has done in three years. I desire to take the most emphatic issue with my right hon. friend on that point. I do not understand the motive which led him to make such an assertion, having regard to 'his responsibility as a public man and to the position that he occupies in this House and in this country. I desire to draw no comparisons. I fully realize the splendid effort that the United States is making in this war; I have heard many accounts of it in recent days. There is no doubt about the fact that they are making a magnificent effort; they are going into the war in a splendid, whole-hearted way', with a view to achieving the victory which we all desire. But I should like to tell my hon. friend-if he does not know it, he ought to know it-that if the United States had made proportionately the same effort in this war that Canada made in the first two months after the war broke out in 1914, she would have raised within six weeks after she entered the war an army
of 500,000 men, and within two months she would have had that army on the ocean en route to France.
With regard to the whole question, I should like my right hon. friend to realize that this is a war-time election which he has forced on this country. So far as the disqualification of aliens of enemy nationality is concerned, there are some considerations that he has not taken into account. Does my right hon. friend seriously propose that we should put aliens of enemy nationality under the Military Service Act and send them to the front line of trenches in France and Flanders to fight men of their own kin, men of their own blood, men, perhaps, with whom they were brought up in the days gone by? If my right hon. friend says that we should call upon them to- pronounce judgment upon the issue of this war in this election, will he shrink from declaring that they ought to be subject to the same military service as other citizens of Canada? If he takes the one position, it seems to me that he must take the other. He has taken care, however, not to put that forward, for reasons which are very obvious. It would be unnatural to send these men to the front to fight those of their own flesh and blood. Indeed, it would be cruel to do so, because the naturalization which they have obtained in Canada does not follow them after they leave the limits of this country, and if they were sent to the front line trenches and were captured by the German or Austrian troops, they might he shot. Would any man say that under those circumstances we should force these men into combatant military service; that we should send them into the front line of battle to fight against their own flesh and blood? Moreover, if we were disposed to take that extraordinary course, what result would follow? The military authorities at the front would not permit us to do. so. I have not one word to say against the loyalty to Canada of these men. Throughout this war they have conducted themselves, on the whole, in a reasonable and orderly manner. But no one can doubt that the ties of blood mean something to them, as they do to us. No one can doubt that these men do have a certain sympathy with those of their own kin who are fighting against our troops in the trenches beyond the seas. While on the whole there might not he the danger which is apprehended by the military authorities, who would undertake to say that in some individual instance a man's intense sym-

pathy for his. own flesh and blood might not overcome hie loyalty to hie adopted country? If that occurred in one, two, or three instances, what would be the result? If my right hon. friend had seen some of the telegrams that I have read in regard to what happened to some of the New Zealand troops overseas eighteen months ago, he would, perhaps, realize that considerations of this kind are entitled to more weight than he has been disposed to give them.
If I have made good my point that it is absolutely impracticable for ns to force these men into combatant service, to send them into the front line trenohek to fight against their own flesh and blood, what follows? What is to be the issue in this election? The issue in this election is to be upon Canada's part in this war, upon the necessity of sending reinforcements to our men overseas who are holding there the first battle line of Canada. The question is as tO' maintaining Canada's effort. If these citizens, by their origin, by their early environment, by the ties of kinship, by their natural sympathies, cannot be forced into the front line to fight, for precisely the same reason they ought not to be called upon to pronounce judgment upon the issues which [DOT]will he to the fore in this election. They do not want to be forced into combatant service; more than that, I have reason to believe, from statements that have come to me from most reliable sources, that a large number of these men will be grateful for exemption from compulsory military service on the one hand and for not being called upon to pronounce their judgment in this election on the other. For the same reason that they do not wish to be sent to the front line to fight against their own kindred, they do not wish to be forced into the disagreeable alternative of pronouncing a. judgment in which, on the one hand, there is a question of their devotion to their adopted country and to its national purposes, and on the other hand, there is the force of ties of kinship and sympathy towards those who are fighting against us. These considerations apply equally to German-speaking citizens from Russia, whose origin, kinship and sympathies are subject to the same observations, although technically they were citizens of an Allied nation.
My right hon. friend has developed a very deep and sudden sympathy for granting the franchise to the women of this country. I had understood, even until the middle cf the present session, that my right hon.
£Sir Robert Borden.]
friend was not very sympathetic to that proposal, and that some of his followers had much difficulty in persuading my right hon. friend that he should come to their view. He starts out on the assumption that the women of Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia are entitled to vote at federal elections. I take direct issue with him on that point. I say they are not entitled, under the present law, to vote at federal elections. Therefore, when my right hon. friend argues that we are depriving those women of a vote to which they are presently entitled, he is speaking without the book, if we rely, as we are entitled to rely, upon the opinions of the law officers of the Crown and of all authorities whom we have consulted on that question. I should further like to point out to my right \hon. friend and to those on the other side of the House that the question of conferring the franchise on all the women of Canada is surrounded with certain difficulties and complexities which, in my judgment, cannot be solved within the four remaining weeks which comprise the lifetime of this Parliament. In receiving the franchise, women assume an equal status with men in directing and controlling the Government of this country. That is the logical and inevitable consequence of their gradual emancipation from the days when the personality of a woman was absolutely merged in that of her husband, and when women were regarded as not entitled to any voice either in the affairs of the country, or even with regard to their own property. They were denied the right to make contracts. They were not looked upon in the same light as were men in the direction of the affairs of the State, or even in the direction of their own personal affairs. We have emerged from all that. We are emerging now to the point at which the women of this country must be entitled to the same voice in directing the affairs of the country as men, and so far as I am concerned, I commit myself absolutely to that proposal:	But I say,
that in working it out, it is necessary to take into account certain considerations. I happen to know that the women of this country themselves are very much alive to those considerations. The consideration is this: that the citizenship of a married woman is not dependent, under the law of this country, upon any individual application on her behalf for naturalization, but her citizenship-with one trifling exception which became law for the first time ini 1914

is dependent upon the citizen-

ship of her husband. The result of that is this: After the 1st day of January next no man is entitled to naturalization in this country unless he shall -have resided in this country for five years. The law up to the -present time has required -a residence of three years. But if a woman from the Balkan states or elsewhere comes into this country, and after a three weeks' or three months' residence, marries a man who is a native-born or naturalized British subject, she at once becomes -a British subject herself. Therefore, unless some safeguard is provided, the alien woman who marries a native-born or naturalized British subject would become entitled to the franchise with no residence at all, or with a residence very far -short of that required of men. Every hon. gentleman will realize that such a result would require pretty careful examination and study by Parliament. I say again that the women of this country are very much alive to that consideration, -and delegations of women from both East- and West have pressed it upon my attention. What is the remedy for that condition? The Tem-edy, it seems to me, is this: If a woman is to have -an equal status with a man in the franchise and in determining the direction of public affairs in this country, is it not reasonable that a woman shall have an equal voice in determining what her citizenship -shall be? If she is entitled to -a full voice in the direction of public affairs she is entitled to an equally full voice in deciding what her citizenship shall be. What is the law at the present 'time? A woman who has resided in Canada all her life marries an -alien in this country, and what happens? She loses her British citizenship. That is not a fair result if we are to grant the franchise to women. Suppose we should grant the franchise to all the women of Canada to-morrow and leave the naturalization law as it is -at present. Then any British-born woman, any woman born within the limits of this Empire, resident in Canada, who might marry an alien, would immediately lose her right to vote because her citizenship would become the citizenship of her husband. Therefore, we must consider the provisions of the naturalization law, and w-e must give to -alien women who come into Canada a right to individual^iaturalization, which they cannot have under the law as it is to-day.
My right hon. friend will say: Why not do that at the present session? ,1 say: It is
impossible, in view of the brevity of the time remaining at our disposal, to give that question the attention and to surround the measure with the safeguards necessary f-or that purpose. Let us remember that -in 1914 -a very earnest, and, I think, -an effective attempt was made for two purposes, One was to have a uniform naturalization law passed in the Mother Country and in every great Dominion of the Empire. The Other was to increase the length of residence in various Dominions of the Empire for the purpose of naturalization -and to make such naturalization effective throughout -the Empire. The law which was passed in 1914 in Great Britain was passed by this Parliament as well. It was .passed, -also, by the legislature of the colony of Newfoundland. I -am not sure whether it was enacted in any of the .other self-governing Dominions. I think it was passed by one other, but I am not certain. It is not apparent that if we are to amend our naturalization law, as seems to be necessary, in order that women may have the right individually to determine their citizenship, we must -have some negotiation, we must give careful consideration to the purpose of uniformity which inspired the Imperial Conference of 1911, to -take -steps along this line? We have a naturalization law which is in precisely the same terms as that in force in the British Islands and in Newfoundland, and possibly in some other Dominions. The purpose is to -have that Naturalization Act uniform throughout the whole Empire and to make it effective throughout. It is impossible for us to accomplish the purpose which, I think, is necessary, and which, I believe, the women of Canada consider necessary, in the few weeks yet remaining in the life of this Parliament.
W'hat have we done under the circumstances? We have determined that we shall give to all the women of Canada who have immediate relatives serving in the Canadian Expeditionary Force the right to a voice in this election. Who shall deny them that right? It is based upon precisely the- same principle as that which guided this Parliament in determining the qualifications under the Military Voters' Act, because men to-day serving in the Canadian Expeditionary Force have a right to vote at the impending election who would not have that right if they had not joined that force. The principle upon which we . have proceeded is, as the Secretary of State properly expressed it the other day, the principle of service and of sacrifice.
