There are other and additional considerations. Three hundred thousand men of the best that Canada can produce have joined the Canadian Expeditionary Force and gone overseas to fight for our liberties and our institutions. Is any hon. gentleman in this House inclined to minimize the influence which those men could exert during the coming election if they were personally present in Canada? Is not some regard and some importance to be attached to that consideration? But there is more than that. It will depend entirely upon the military operations as to how many of these men will have the opportunity to vote, and it is beyond question that many thousands of them by reason of the service in which they are offering themselves for the supreme sacrifice will not have that opportunity. But there is more than that. Thirty thousand of them lie buried in France and Flanders, and is it not right that the immediate relatives of these men should have some voice to speak on their behalf when the issues at the next election come to be determined? There are also some thousands of them prisoners in Germany, undergoing hardship and privation, to whom it is impossible to give the opportunity to vote at the impending election. Is it not right that some one in this country should have the opportunity to speak on their behalf? There are thousands of these men in the British or allied forces who were residents of Canada and would have had the right to vote at the next election except for this war and the service they are giving.
I deem it right that some person in this country should have the right to speak in their behalf.
I say that this proposal to extend the franchise to the immediate relatives of soldiers at the front is not only a fair and reasonable proposal, but I go further and say that it would be most unfair and unjust if some one did not have the right to speak on their behalf. These are the reasons and the considerations which have impelled the Government to propose this measure to Parliament. The voice of those who are serving Canada overseas, of those who have fallen, of those who have died in order that Canada might live, of those who lie in German prisons, that voice we are endeavouring to preserve and give effect to by this measure.

Mr. Speaker, I understand the Prime Minister to say that the introduction of this Bill was largely brought about by the refusal to extend the life of Parliament. I 
was one of those who- voted against the extension of the life of this Parliament, and also one of those who voted in favour of the Military Service Act. I also represent a constituency where there are a number of people who belong to the nationalities that will be deprived of the franchise by this measure. When I voted for conscription, when I voted against the extension of the life of Parliament, I realized that I would have 'to face these people and explain my position. But I was satisfied and I am satisfied still that I could appeal to them and present reasons for the attitude I took and get their support. But now, with a measure of this character before tne House, I cannot go to them and appeal for their support. I have appealed to them ever since this war commenced on behalf of the Patriotic Fund and other patriotic causes; I have explained to them why we are engaged in this war; I have pointed out to them that we were fighting for freedom, liberty and justice, fighting for the national honour and for the pledged word. Now I cannot go back to them and say: "I have urged you to support this cause and to be loyal to this country," and then defend a course that would mean that I, a member of this Parliament, had broken the pledged word of Canada to these people when they became citizens of this country. That is my position. I do not think it is fair for this Parliament to charge that every man of German or Austrian, birth in this country is disloyal. I know men who- are not of those nationalities ; some of them \ are Canadian-born; yes, and some of them are British-born, and. they have not displayed any great loyalty to this country or to our Allies since this war commenced. Why should they also not be deprived of the franchise?
I read a certain paper day in and day out, and have done so since this war commenced. It is the greatest exponent of the cause of the Allies on the American continent, if not in the whole world, and it is published by a man who was born in Germany; I refer to the New York Times. There is another paper published in the city of New York, the New York World, founded, I think, by a man of Austrian birth, and published to-day by his son, which is a'lso ,#n exponent of the cause of the Allies. And who did the President of the United States depend upon to carry his selective draft measure through the House of Representatives at Washington? When the Democratic leader in that body, a man,

I think, not of foreign birth at any rate, refused to promote that measure in the House of Representatives, the ranking Republican, a man of German extraction, if not a German-born, a Congressman from California, directed the measure through that House. And is it fair in this' Parliament of Canada, where v?e maintain we are fighting for freedom, liberty and justice, and where we have given these people the rights of citizenship, that we should stamp upon every one of them who came to this country and became citizens since 1902 the mark of disloyalty, and say that they are not prepared to do their part as citizens of this country? I say, no.
This measure is largely directed against the people who are living in western Canada, against the people who have become citizens since 1902. The settlers of German birth in Ontario who came prior to that are left with the franchise. Now if I remember rightly there have been more expressions of disloyalty amongst some of these people in the province of Ontario than there have been throughout the whole West since this war commenced, and still you are leaving these people in Ontario and the older parts of eastern Canada with a vote, and taking away from the new settlers in western Canada the rights we guaranteed them as citizens. These people have been urged to Temain loyal and respect our laws from the commencement of this war, and most of them have done so.
I publish a newspaper in the southern part of the province of Alberta. My ambition has been to create a national senti ment amongst all our new citizens. In my newspaper and during the opportunities I have had as a public man I have done all that I could to promote a virile Canadian sentiment. I was today looking over the report of the Commissioners of the Royal Northwest Mounted police for the year 1916, and in nearly every instance the officials connected with the Royal Northwest Mounted Police say they have had practically no trouble whatever with the foreign-born element in western Canada.
I was speaking at the commencement of my remarks of the attitude taken by myself as a western member on the question of conscription, but my position is far easier than that of many men from western Canada who voted for the Military Service Bill. Compared with some western members who voted for conscription, I have very few of the foreign element
in my constituency. These hon. members [DOT]knew they had these people in their constituencies, but they voted for conscription nevertheless. It was a very drastic war measure, but these men broke with their party and supported it, although they knew that back in their constituencies there were hundreds and thousands of foreign-bom citizens. I would refer to the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely), the member for Saltcoats (Mr. MacNutt), and the members for many other constituencies, who are in a far different position from myself.
Still, this Government practically repudiates the independence of the western Liberal members who stood up for the Selective Military Measure in this House, and who broke with their party on that question, and they introduce a measure which practically says they have no confidence in many of our constituents.
I want to say that hon. gentlemen on this side of the	House who
voted for this measure have confidence in their constituents, no matter to what race they may belong. So far as I am concerned, as a member of this House who supported conscription, if I am to go before my constituents again, I will tell them, whether they are foreignrborn, Canadian-born or British-born, that I supported conscription because I thought it was right, and that they can only elect me on the understanding .that I will continue to support conscription and maintain the law in force until the completion of the war. That is my position. The attitude the Government is taking at this time is most unfair, and it is a slap in the face to every western Liberal member who supported this Government on conscription.
We left our party and we took the position we did for the national advantage, because we looked upon the measure as a war measure. This Government is adopting the present measure not as a war measure and not for the national advantage, but for the advantage of the party they represent. I would like to say, that, if we are going to build up a united Canada,	if we	are	going to bring
people into this country and promise them the rights of citizenship, we must adhere to the pledged word we have given them. We must let them know that while we are fighting autocracy, while we are fighting a nation that broke its word to another nation, we as Canadians, living under the British flag, are going to adhere

to our word. If we trust these people, and if we let them understand the position of Canada and the position of the Allies, I think we can appeal to them and that they will stand loyally by us. Hundreds and thousands of them came away from their home countries because they objected to the form of Government, and because they were oppressed. Seeking relief, they came to Canada. They may not be anxious to support militarism of any kind in this countt-y-as a matter of fact, many of them are opposed to war-but at the same time, many of them are opposed to the position taken in this war by the countries from which they came, and to the part those countries are taking in the war.
There is another feature of the Act to which I wish to refer briefly. The right to vote has been given to women, on the ground of war service or war sacrifice. 1 heartily approve of that feature of the Act. but I agree with many others who have spoken, from this side of the House at any rate, that war service or war sacrifice has not been confined solely to the women who allowed their loved ones to go across the *sea and participate in the war, and probably sacrifice their lives for us. There are many women throughout the length and breadth of the country, in the cities, in the towns, in the villages, and in the farm homes, who have sacrificed much of their time, who have sewed and knitted and contributed for patriotic causes. In
5 p.m. my judgment that element of our population should have been included in this Act, and they could very well have been included. If it is war service the Government is anxious to recognize, and if it is the friends of the Allies they 'want to recognize, why do not our friends from the province of British Columbia advocate that the franchise should be given to the Japanese and the Chinese there? They are our allies. They are fighting for us at the present time. If you are going to deprive a certain element of our population of their franchise-
Does my hon. friend recommend that the' franchise should be given to the Japanese?
Order.

The Government would have as much right to do that as they have to disfranchise those citizens of Canada who took the oath of allegiance to this country, and who promised to he loyal and obedient citizens. If this were a question of war service, I believe, so far as the provisions 
relating to the franchise for women are concerned, the Government should have been more generous, and should have included all the war workers. What have we to say about those women who have been working in the munition factories since the war commenced? What have we to say about the young women who are giving their time driving automobile trucks around the city of Ottawa, for instance, for patriotic purposes? Are they not serving their country, and are they not making sacrifices? Why should they not be recognized? To my mind it is only absolutely fair that they should have recognition.
Certainly the next of kin of our soldiers have a right to be recognized, but it would have been a happy thing for this Parliament to have extended the privilege to every woman who has played her part as a patriotic citizen since the war started. I believe we can only create a proper spirit of unity throughout this country by placing trust in the people we have brought here and to whom we have given the rights of citizenship. We cannot create unity by looking upon them with suspicion, and by depriving them of the rights we guaranteed them when they became citizens, because in doing so we practically contradict the position we have' taken as a participant in this war. We have always held the ground that Canada was in the war for great principles, one of which was respect for the pledged word and the maintenance of national honour. We cannot expect to have the loyal support of our citizens if we abandon that principle, and refuse to recognize our pledged word.
I also object to the measure because it does not give a sufficiently broad franchise to the women of this country, and I will oppose it on those grounds.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
There is a disposition on the part of opponents of this measure to describe it as a disfranchisement measure, and to ascribe to it peculiarities which they seem to think are traditional with the Tory party.
It is no disfranchisement measure, except in a very small and limited sense. On the contrary its enfranchisement features so far transcend its disfranchisement features that, taken in all, it is in comparison to our population, the widest extension of the franchise ever passed by a British community.
The hon. member who has just sat down (Mr. Buchanan), for the sincerity of whose opinions I have the most profound respect, appears to be labouring

under the apprehension that in this measure there is some rebuke to those hon. gentlemen opposite who supported the Government on the question of conscription. For the life of me I do not understand by what process of reasoning he arrives at that conclusion. The vote of no hon. member in this House would have been more welcome to the Administration of the day than that of the hon. member for Lethbridge, if he could have brought himself to the conclusion that this measure was right. Our only motive in introducing this measure is to safeguard the franchise of this country in a perilous crisis, in the interests of the Canadian people, and for no party advantage at all. I would like to know what party advantage can come to members on this side of the House by the passing of this measure which would not accrue to the hon. member for Lethbridge on exactly the same score. If it hurts us, it hurts him if he goes to his electors as a conscrip-tionist. If it benefits'us, it benefits him, if he submits himeslf to his constituents on that subject. His views differ from ours as to the merits of the measure. For his views I have respect. But I would ask him to review the sentence in which he ascribed to us motives of animosity and of repudiating or rebuking conscriptionist Liberals on the other side.
I opened with the assertion that this was the widest measure of enfranchisement proportionate to population ever passed by a British community since the first Reform Bill. We disfranchise, it is true, a number of citizens. That is quite correct. We disfranchise them temporarily while this war lasts. The number of disfranchised is estimated by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. MoGraney) as about thirty thousand; my own judgment would place it higher, but there is no way of getting at anything like the exact figures. But we enfranchise, of those who would not get the vote at all if this measure were not passed, not less, in my judgment, than 400,000, perhaps 500,000 or moie of the population of this country. Thus an estimate of 470,000 net addition to the electorate as a result of this measure if it passes Parliament is not far out of the way.
The Bill has two features. I take the first feature in my initial argument, the enfranchising feature, which gives the franchise to the near female relatives of the soldiers overseas. That is objected to by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan) on the ground that it is not strictly the line of service that is recognized, that there is a service on the part of womankind beyond the service of the woman whose husband, or brother, or father is fighting overseas. I agree that there is such a service, but the extent of service and the character of the sacrifice which the woman makes who works in a munitions factory, or knits, or sews, is not the same as that of the woman whose husband's, or whose brother's, life is in peril. The hon. member for Lethbridge takes very good care-and he does so advisedly and wisely, in my judgment-to speak no word that could be construed as committing him to the unlimited enfranchisement of women in this country at the present time. He wants to make the line of all service the line of franchise. How are we to tell, how could it be made practicable, to add to those whose near relatives are overseas those who knit and sew and attend Red Cross meetings and visit the afflicted? Could we ever draw .such a line and establish it by legislation? He knows it is impracticable. He knows that we have to take a broad and general line, even although cases of individual injustice arise. We cannot enfranchise by individuals; we must enfranchise by classes. We draw the line where it can easily and clearly be drawn, at those who make the greatest and the highest sacrifice, and we say that, for the purposes of this war, that line is the most logical, the most defensible. Some line has to be drawn; no better line than that can be drawn.
It is argued as well that we throw a slur or cast some ignominy on those who do not enjoy the franchise under this Bill. I cannot agree with this reasoning. They were compared, in the language of the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. McCraney), to the negroes of the southern states. Why, it is only two or three months since, in this House, we were favoured with a resolution moved by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) that for the franchise of Canada we should adopt the provincial franchise, twith female voters, 'which would have enfranchised the women of five provinces and refused the franchise to those of the other four! Were the women of the other four under his proposal to be likened to the negroes of the southern states? Not at all; but they would have been, if the reasoning of the hon. member for Saskatoon is correct.
We said at that time that Whatever franchise was adopted for women should be Canada-wide, and should be enjoyed through all the provinces; and that prin-

eiple is embodied in ibis Bill. We favoured that motion, provided there were such limitations as Parliament ishould afterwards deem to be fitting. These are the limitations, and let those who dispute the justibe or logic of these limitations suggest others to the members of this House. The reasoning of the Prime Minister this afternoon is conclusive. We could not go to the extent, under existing conditions, of enfranchising all the women of Canada. To do so would give no special representative vote to the overseas soldiers-in lieu of what an election now denies them. The women of Canada did not ask for the enfranchisement at this time of all the women. They have approached members of this Government and have protested against such a wide enfranchisement, because they felt that under the conditions of this war, with our heterogeneous population, the votes of those foremost in the women's suffrage movement would be defeated ' by the votes of those scattered throughout our country w'ho are affected by sympathies not at all the same as those which actuate the great bulk of the women of this country.
The Bill denies qualificatioh for the period of this war to those of alien enemy birth *who have been naturalized since March 31, 1902, and to those of alien enemy blood, born in other countries and speaking the language of an alien enemy. It is contended vigorously on the part of the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) that this is un-British, that it is a breach of a pledge given by this country, ana that, whatever the consequence, we must not do this thing. I should like to know where that pledge is printed, where it was given. I have never seen it. I have seen pledges given to immigrants; they are embodied in Orders in Council. There have been pledges given exempting certain immigrants from military service in this country. Those pledges we respect. Any pledge given we respect. But no pledge has ever *been given to immigrantsi in this country that is repudiated by this Bill.

When any man is naturalized and becomes a naturalized British subject, is he not given a pledge to the effect that "he is, within Canada, entitled to- all political and other rights, powers and privileges to which a natural-born British subject is entitled?"

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, but it adds that at the same time they must assume all our obligations. Does the hon. member say

that, under that, there cannot be a limitation of the franchise? If so, how does he justify the Government of Saskatchewan, which he supports, and which disfranchised British subjects, naturalized, coming from China?
What has that to do with this?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: If there is a pledge, is not that pledge violated by that Act?
Let us grant, for the sake of argument, that the legislature did very wrong.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I have not heard the hon. member complain of that legislature doing wrong in this matter. Why? Because he never until to-day interpreted naturalization in such a way.
A pretty weak argument.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The rights of British subjects here are rights given under the law of Canada. The law of Canada must be dictated by the needs of the hour, foT the safety of Canada. Does the hon. member say that in British Columbia there has been a breach of faith because for years past, if not since the birth of that province, they have refused the franchise to British subjects naturalized by the very same certificate, the Japanese and men of alien birth? Is it a breach of faith that those two provinces have done this for years? There is not a shadow of a breach of faith.

I understand we were
discussing whether Canada was breaking its pledged word, and I read the naturalization form from the Act.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Let the hon. member
say that two provinces of Canada have dishonoured their pledged word since those two provinces were created. He will not say it; he knows it is not true.
Were those people naturalized?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Certainly.
By the provinces?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: By the Dominion.

They had no
political rights.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Now we have a beautiful political distinction drawn by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean), and approved by the hon. member for Renfrew (Mr. Graham), that the pledged word of this country given to immigrants in Canada may not be vio-

lated by the Dominion Parliament, but may be violated by provincial legislatures. Is the pledged word of Canada not of any moment to provincial legislatures? Does it mean nothing to them? The pledged word of this country is not violated any more by their legislation than it is by this -Parliament now? There are others who were disfranchised in this country. They had not been likened to negroes before. Judges have no vote. Many British-born people have no vote. It is true this is the widest measure of the kind that has yet been placed on the statue book. It is abnormal. But we live in abnormal times. Hon. gentlemen opposite say these people have obeyed the law, and are all right. It is true that, in the main, they obey the law, and there has been little exception, all things considered, to the manner in which they have lived up to their obligations as citizens, but is it seriously argued by those who know these men coming from Germany and Austria, naturalized within the last fifteen years in Canada, are animated by the same sympathy in this war, as animates us, that, as a class, are anxious for Britain to win this war, and that they look upon the dread issue of this struggle in the same light as we? Let me put a case to hon. gentlemen opposite, and to the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laur-ier). Let me assume that one of the hon. gentlemen opposite goes abroad, in order to better his condition in the world. He goes to some European land. He takes up his abode there, and enters on a homestead. In order to get his patent, he has to take out naturalization papers in three - years. After he is there a few years, a war breaks out between that country and his native land. He looks across, and finds his own brothers, and perhaps his own children, perhaps his father, his very next of kin, fighting in the armies of his native land, against that of his adopted country. Does any one want to seriously state to this Parliament that tsuch a man would look upon the issue of that struggle as would his neighbours of the blood of his adopted land? Does any one suggest he would be animated by the same desire for the triumph of the army of his adopted country, as would those next door to him, who were of the blood of that adopted land? Human nature is human nature in us all, and is human nature in the German and Austrian in Canada. Would the right hon. gentleman want to be conscripted in that country to
fight against his sons at home? Would he expect to be loaded down with the obligations of that war, as would his brothers fighting on the other side? I do not think he would. I do not think he would complain if relieved of those obligations in that country, he was refused a say in the direction of that war.
Is it true that in South Africa there were complaints, because at no time, tho-ugli . they took a large measure in the obligations of the country, were British subjects entitled to the franchise. But who that wants to be reasonab'e, would contend for a moment that, if the Transvaal had been at war with Great Britain, and if, during that war, and for the purposes of that war alone British subjects by birth naturalized in the Transvaal had been refused the franchise, that that would have been looked on as a breach of faith by us? Does any one conceive such an argument? Not at all. Th-e franchise of peace time i-s founded on peace service and the franchise of war times is founded on war service. It is said by hon. gentlemen opposite, " Oh, we are as anxious to win this war as you are. This election is only being fought on the question of the best method to pursue to win the war." If the election has to be fought on the best method to pursue to win the war, why do-es the leader of the Opposition express so keen a desire to get the opinion of those who- do not want to win the war at all, who cannot be expected by -all principles of human nature to welcome the prospect of their brothers being slaughtered that our sons and brothers may triumph.
It is strenuously argued that this is a breach of faith? Did Australia commit a breach of faith? Is Australia blackened by the crime of Germany, because Australia deemed, under the circumstances of -this war, that, as the obligations of war were lifted from the immigrants of alien enemy birth in that country, the privileges of the franchise mutt be lifted as well? Does any one say that the crime of the " scrap of paper " must be laid -at the do-o-r of Australia? Such a thing never was suggested in the Australian House. A similar measure wider in its terms than this Bill, passed the Australian Parliament, almost without protest at all, and they disfranchised every man of alien enemy birth, no matter when he came to the country.

Why do
you start with 1902 in dealing with these people?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Unless we went back indefinitely, unless we disqualified those wh.o-
Is that what Australia did?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: She went back indefinitely.
If you followed the Australian precedent in one respect, why not follow it right through?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Because we think they went too far. Would the hon. gentleman go as far as they went? We strike a middle line. Australia disfranchised those who came to that country, no matter when they came. We say that if men have been in this country so long that one can reasonably expect that they have become, as it were, engrafted in the tree of Canada, that they feel as we feel, though perhaps not to the same degree, still to some safe degree, then we believe they are entitled to assume the war obligations of this country, and entitled to assume the franchise in war time.
Is there any precedent in England for war-time franchise?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: They have had no wartime election-there is no precedent irt England of a party forcing a war-time election.
Are elections not being held continually, all through the war, in England?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
A few by-elections, but no general elections, and Great Britain is 95 to 98 per cent British-horn,, while we have a very substantial proportion of alien enemy birth.
It has also been vigorously asserted-although I do not know that we should be troubled by it, because there has never been an important measure introduced in Parliament with regar^l to which the same thing has not been asserted-that this is a partisan measure, designed to re-elect this Government. I desire to remind particularly the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. McCraney), and the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Buchanan) that the same thing has been asserted just as vigorously, just as consistently, and indeed, infinitely more strenuously with regard to the conscription measure of this Government. From one end of Canada to the other, those who do not want to further help the soldiers in France state that the reason we desired to

pass such a measure was that we wanted to get back to power.
The argument now is based on the theory laid down by the hon. member for iSaeka-toon (Mr. McCraney), that those we enfranchise will support us, and that those we disqualified will oppose us. They charge repeatedly against us that such is our belief. If it is true-and apparently it is true, if hon. gentlemen opposite are right-that the majority of the women, of (this country whose near relatives are overseas, those who spend their days in anxiety and their nights in f tears, will support us, and that those who, of all our population, are likely to favour the enemy, will reject us, then, in the name of the Government which has been striving for three years to fight that enemy, I accept the compliment.
I do believe that the majority of those in the trenches will support the Administration. I do believe also that the majority of those whose near relatives are overseas fighting the foe would rather support this Administration than support one formed by the leader of the Opposition. I further believe that those at the other end of the electoral thermometer, those whose sympathies, whose very heart-strings, are by nature tied to the enemy, are much more likely to support the leader of the Opposition than to support us. But I do not believe that that is an argument against this Bill; I do not believe that Liberals and Conservatives generally throughout Canada, or even those who are disqualified temporarily during war time, will oo regard this measure. I have received communications from rften who will be disqualified by this Bill-from men with whom I had had not the slightest communication on the subject until the Bill was brought down. I have received a communication from one of the leading members of a disfranchised community in the western country, in which he commended the Government for the action taken, saying that it removed the whole community from the embarrassing position in which it was placed by reason of the war We have been waited upon by representatives of communities of aliens; the Government has been urged that this stop be taken. Representations to this end have been made by Liberals who want to see this war carried on; who do not want to see Canada slink from the field. I know that instinctively the Liberal mind-and instinctively our own mind, because our own mind in. the best sense is liberal-does not

like the idea of disfranchisement. We should be glad if it were not necessary; yet I know scores of persons, who though at first resisting this measure or any measure of this kind, have since made the declaration that they believe the measure essential and right, and that they will support it. These words apply particularly to Liberals; if any hon. gentleman opposite desires me to name them, I shall be glad to do so at any time. I think that the great bulk of Liberals in this country who are anxious to go on and not to- go back will. support the measure that is now before the House.

Mr. Speaker, I should be failing in my duty if I did not res-e-nt with every particle of strength in my being -the uncalled for, unjustifiable, unrighteous insult offered to a laTge number of the people whom I~repre-sent by the proposals embodied in this Bill and by the statements made by the Secretary of State (Mr. Meighen) upon its introduction. Like other members of this House, I recognize the ability as a debater of the Secretary of State-some say he is a hair-splitter-but I never saw him make such a shamefaced performance as he did when he introduced this Franchise Bill the other day. It was the utterance of a man who was ashamed, Sir, of what he was doing. I give him credit-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member should resume his seat when the Speaker rises. The hon. member is certainly exceeding the rules of debate; I would ask him to take more cognizance of them.

I shall have to keep myself within the rules-, but I may tell you frankly, Mr. Speaker, that when several hundreds of my constituents, as loyal a people as there are in Canada, are being insulted by the Secretary of State, I find it very difficult to observe the rules of debate and of parliamentary procedure. I should like to know wherein I make an unfair comment when I say that in my judgment the performance of the Secretary of State when he introduced this measure was that of a man who was ashamed of what he was doing.
Mr. SPEAKER; The hon. member uses unparliamentary language w-hen he addresses that remark -to the Secretary of State. He is at liberty to characterize the measure as he wishes, provided 'he uses parliamentary language. But !he is not in order when he applies such a remark to the Secretary of State.

Well, I have -said what
I had to -say on that point, anyway. If you are willing, Mr. -Speaker, I will pass on to the next.
Sir -GEORGE FOSTER: I think that my hon.' friend, having said something of a member that he should not have said, and having been called to order for doing so, should have withdrawn the assertion.

Mr. Speaker, whil-e I am
willing to accept your ruling in -respect to anything that I have said, I do not want any lecture from the Minister of Trade and Commerce as to what is right and what is wrong in parliamentary procedure.

Mr. Speaker, I
ask that the-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I took the statement of the hon. member for Humboldt as a withdrawal, -and consequently I did not ask for a retraction in terms.

One of the chief reasons
put forward by the Secretary of State, for the disfranchisement of a certain class -of people in this country was that it was in the interests of the safety of the State, that such a course should be taken. Does that not mean that a certain class of citizens in Canada are not to be trusted with the franchise? If a certain class of the citizens of this country cannot be trusted with the franchise at this time, then my hon. friend had better include -in 'that class-after all, the election is to be held upon the question of method as to winning th-e war-the thousands of British, English, French, Scotch, -Canadian-born in this country who, if a referendum on conscription were submitted to the people to-morrow, would vote against any such measure. If only men who come within the jurisdiction of the Military Service measure are to be given the franchise, then a large number of the members of this Hous-e would be disfranchised. Every man over forty-five years of -age would be disfranchised.
Mr. PU'GSLEY: Even the Solicitor-General.

Those were the reasons given-considerations of loyalty and the question of military service. If disloyalty means nothing more than voting against this Government because they have brought m a measure of compulsor-y service, my hon. friend will find, -before the election is over, that there are tens of thousands, aye, hundreds of thousands of people in Canada
Hear, hear.

In these two statements, coupled with the "hear, hear" of the hon. gentlemen who hope to profit politically by this Bill, is the proof that the Bill was introduced solely for partisan purposes, and that neither nearly nor remotely has it anything to do with the winning of the war. On the contrary, its effect will be to retard much of the noble effort which has heretofore been put forth by people in the Dominion of Canada who are not sufficiently fortunate to have members of their family at tlie front. There are four classes affected

by this Bill: aliens of enemy origin; men who do not believe in war; women who are enfranchised; women who are refused the franchise. The women who are refused the franchise are put in the same class with the men who do not want to fight, and with the alien enemy; and the Government can give us all the sophistry it chooses as to why these women are not given the right to vote, but it still remains sophistry. The Government does not believe that these women would vote for them in an election, and	that is the	reason
why they are not given the franchise. This is in line with the argument of the Solicitor General. Let me take up, first, those of alien enemy origin. The situation is this. The Government says to the man who has remained truly loyal under very severe conditions: "We will place upon your-brow . and upon the brows of your children the brand of disloyalty and treachery, and the shame of it will follow you as long as you live, while we who have remained loyal because this is our mother country and it is easy for us to be loyal, will smite our breasts and thank God we are not as other men, or even as those aliens who remain loyal under present circumstances." The reward the Government proposes to give to those men who remain loyal under present trying conditions is to deprive them of the citizenship which has been guaranteed to them. I ask hon. gentile-men is that an incentive to loyalty? Does it tend .to breed patriotism among newcomers to this country? Will it impress upon the mind of the newcomer the fairness of British institutions? Will it show that we are the exemplars of the purest liberty under the sun? It gives a directly contrary impression, and I say now that this act of the Government will do more to cause unrest and to create misgivings -among those who come from foreign lands to Canada than anything that has happened since Confederation. And, further, it will do more to retard immigration into Canada than anything this Government or any other Government could do. The Prime Minister went through the West on a laudable tour, making patriotic speeches. We all read those speeches, and thought they would have a good effect. The men to whom they were addressed, as well as their wives, listened to these speeches carefully, and were undoubtedly impressed. What do we find now? The men who listened to those patriotic words spoken throughout our 
western country-the men who came to the head of -this Government, the Prime Minister of Canada, to gain from him knowledge of the freedom for which we were fighting, knowledge of the genius of our constitution, knowledge of those rights which come to every man who takes up citizenship under the Union Jack-these men went home, and profited by tho.se words. They did their best for the cause, rejoicing in the freedom which they had. And now they are branded as traitors, without any explanation or reason being given to this House ar to the country. This Bill not only disfranchises men of -alien enemy origin who have come to this country since 1902, but it disfranchises many men in the province of Ontario, who have been -among our very best citizens for the last thirty or forty years, men whose taxation for carrying on the war is great, men whose wives have laboured early and late, men who have sacrificed much, and -som-e men whose -sons are at the front. If this other clause had not been put in-	_

Let me explain what I mean, because objection will be immediately taken to this-

I will clear up the
point in -a moment. There are men in this country who came from other lands, took up their residence .here, and for twenty years they have been voting in Canada. Hon. members in this House can call them by name. They are good citizens, and they believed they had the right to vote. That right of citizenship was never questioned by either side of politics. When this war -broke out, they discovered that, although they had been voting for many years, they had never gone through the formality of becoming naturalized. Being loyal citizens, and to show that they were true to the Union Jack and the British Empire, they immediately took out their naturalization papers. But they have only been naturalized two or three years. And although they have been building up this country, paying taxes land raising their families although they are a credit to the country, by this Bill they find themselves disfranchised, and marked among their neighbours as men unworthy to he trusted with citizenship.
I want to know if that is going to have a good effect on the people by whom they are surrounded, or on the people in the coun-

tries from which we expect to get immigration in the future.
Now, as to conscientious objectors. It may be said, and it is said, that these men seldom vote anyway. That they do not care to take part in political strife, and that to deprive them of their franchise is not a very serious matter. For a man to refrain from exercising a right because he wishes to is one thing, but to be deprived of that right by statute is a very different thing; and the man, even although he has not voted, and his son who has voted, will resent for all time to come the interference of this Government which says to them that they are not entitled to exercise the franchise for the election of men to represent them in Parliament and to spend the public revenues to which they contribute. Taxation without representation is one of the things that was fought against at the time of the Family Gompact. We had thought in this country that it had been driven from our shores for all time to come, and it has been the pride of the Canadian people that equal rights have been given to every man, no man being asked to pay taxes unless he is allowed a full voice in the expenditure of those taxes.	Here
are a class of men who contribute largely to the revenues of the country, a class of men who never harm anybody, friendly, peaceful-and they are to be told nbw: You cannot exercise your franchise, and your son cannot exercise his franchise, and in the years to come your son and his sons and daughters will be pointed out, will have the finger of scorn pointed at them throughout the Dominion of Canada as men who, in a crisis in this country, were deemed unworthy to be allowed to exercise the franchise if they had so desired. I say it is an unfair thing, it is a bad business; and although the Secretary of State said this afternoon that he believed the people of Canada would support the Government in this measure, I tell him I believe that he is all wrong, because what is deeply imbedded in the British heart is fair play to everybody and the maxim that everybody is innocent until proven guilty. But this Government undertakes to say that men who are as innocent [DOT]-why, they did not even pretend to make a charge against them-are to be declared guilty without a charge made against them, guilty of a lack of intelligence and integrity such as to unfit them to exercise the franchise. The Von Hollweg of this Government will have to stand side by side with 354
the man who said that a treaty is but a " scrap of paper." The Secretary of State this afternoon argued around that very carefully, as he is capable of doing. But the fact remains that, through ithe Department of the Secretary of State, certain guarantees have been given to men coming to this country, so long as they behave themselves, and one of those guarantees is that they can exercise all political rights. In dishonouring this guarantee, this Government has done just what the Prussian Government did in violating the treaty with Belgium.
Now I come to another class, the women who are enfranchised. The women who are enfranchised, the Secretary of State declares, would number about 500,000; and in palliation of the offence of depriving other citizens of their rights, he declared that the number disfranchised is so infinitesimally small as compared with those enfranchised, that it is not much of a crime after all. Sir, it is not by size or by numbers that the Act will be judged by the people of Canada; it is the principle behind the Act which will bring condemnation on this Government. If only a few were to be disfranchised, then the argument of the Secretary of State that it was necessary to do so for the safety of the State, has no foundation whatever. If the number is so infinitesimally small that it will make no difference in the election, then his argument must go by the board. But he believes, or I think he believes, that this number is so distributed among certain constituencies that it will have the desired effect politically, although in the aggregate the number is not very large. Now, ae to the women who are enfranchised. I am fully in accord with enfranchising women who are closely related to the men who have gone to the front; but I am not in favour of disfranchising those who have no relatives to go to the front but who have done everything they could. The Secretary of State argued that it would be so difficult to get these other women on the list that you would have to make a distinction somewhere; some women you would not dare to put on the list-I have not heard any one say who they were as yet. But I do know that the poor washerwoman who is contributing her fifty cents a week to the Patriotic Fund and has no male relatives to go to the front, is doing all that in her lies for this country, and she should not be deprived of any privilege given to any other women in the Dominion of Canada. In th; - connection, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Gporge Foster) has stood on the platform with myself



i592
on many occasions on behalf of patriotic funds. He has said to the women and to the men: You who cannot go to the front and have no relatives to go to the front can do all that in you lies at home, and your duty will be as fully performed by doing those things as if you were a man and went to the front yourself. To that appeal, made eloquently, as only the Minister of Trade and Commerce can make an appeal, the women of Canada have nobly responded. Day after day, night after night, hour after hour, have they toiled-women in the Red Cross, the Daughters of the Empire, women of other associations, women not attached to any association, knitting by night, sewing by day, preparing comforts for the sons of others, for our sons who are at the front- and, forsooth, this Government says to the woman who is fortunate enough to. be represented at the front: We are going to let you have the vote, but this other woman who has done her part nobly, as did the woman of old, she shall have no voice or lot in the government of this eonntry. Thousands of women have contributed generously to the Red Cross Fund. Many of these women have not representatives at the front; they regret it just as much as any person else can; but they have taken up the burden of the work, they have performed it nobly and well-and this Government, forsooth, draws the line in front of them andi says: You cannot have any voice in running the affairs of this country. I cannot understand the frame of mind that brings men to that conclusion. I have listened carefully to the excuses given for not placing these women on the voters' list-I have yet to find any reason given, they have been mere excuses -and I come back again to this point, that the women who have provided bandages for the boys at the front and have seen them soaked by party heelers as they went through; the women who provided comforts for the boys at the front, and have seen them diverted to other uses across the sea, are so down on this Government that the Government is afraid to trust them with the franchise.
That is a dirty statement.

I repeat that the bandages were soaked in party patronage and rake-off before they got to the soldiers. That has been proven, and I can give the House further evidence of it, if it is desired. The Secretary of State said he believed all these women who were given votes would vote for the Government. I tell him now that he

will find himself mistaken in regard to that. The women of this country know something about the management of public affairs. They want honesty in administration, and if ever there was a time in the history of Canada when the women have taken a deep interest in our affairs, it has been during the past two or three years. They have given up their sons to this cause; if they have no sons to send, they have given up their energy, their effort, their work and their money to aid the Allies. They are watqhing the conduct of public affairs; and the Government will find when the election time comes that, although this Bill has been brought in for party purposes only, the effect expected to be gained will not be gained, but very much the reverse.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman may run into the Senate.

I may say that I have not been trying to run into the Senate yet. I will run wherever there is a fight, because the Government never lets me run without a fight, whatever pledges they make beforehand.
I have had the honour of having the nomination in one riding for twenty-six years, and stayed there. I have never been run out.

I bad the honour of helping to lick the hon. gentleman once. I know that. I should like to direct my attention to the hon. Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White). He has been asking the people to save, and they have been saving. The reward he gives to people for saving is that he becomes a party to a Bill to deprive them of their rights as citizens. Through the Food Controller, the Government has been asking the women of Canada to curtail expenditure. The encouragement to these people, in return for their economy, is that they shall not be allowed to vote unless they comply with certain conditions, which many of them cannot comply with. I want to know what effect that is going to have on the future enthusiasm of these women for war work. I said that this Bill, if it became law, would militate against the progress of the war, and I repeat that statement. The thousands of upright women, rich and poor, who have been labouring hourly, daily, weekly and yearly, in order that success might come to the Allies, find themselves now confronted with the rebuff, the rebuke, the stigma, by this Government, that though they have done all

this they are not entitled to the franchise but must be classed with alien enemies and men who do not want to fight.
