speechtext:
The hon. gentleman's
time is more than up.
I seldom break the rules of the House, and I will not try to break the rule now. I will try and conclude in one word, although it may be a long one.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Not very long.

We ask immigrants to
come to this country. On the success of immigration to Canada depends our ability to meet the financial stress that will come upon us, and this Government has done more by this Bill to cripple us financially than anything that has happened since this Parliament opened.

I am in favour
of the Bill now before the House, for several reasons. First, I arn in favour of it on its merits; and second, I am in favour of it because of the necessities of the war. We have had during this session three important war measures before the House. We have passed the conscription Bill, imposing military duties on all our men of a certain age, because of the necessities of the war. We tried to secure enough men by the voluntary system. We found it impossible to secure them, and, of necessity, we had to pass a conscription law. We owe it to the men who have gone to the front, to pass such a measure, and we also owe it to the men who have died at the front. The great historical precedent for our sending men to the front is that of the Greeks, when they fought for their liberty over 2,500 years ago. 'The people of ISparta sent 300 of their fighting men to Thermopylae, and every one of the 300, with only one exception, was buried on that field of honour, and, to their military glory, a stone was erected, and on that stone was the inscription: Go stranger, tell the Spartans that we lie here, having faithfully observed their commands. Instead of 300 men we have left 30,000 on the warfields of Europe; and we owe it to them to pass this law of compulsory military service. We passed it of necessity. Now, we are passing two other measures, a law to secure the votes of the soldiers, and providing how that vote is to be recorded, and now this law in regard to franchise. Both of these laws were rendered necessary because of the refusal of Parliament to ask for an extension of its life. I am in favour of the Bill now under discussion both because of the additions it makes to the voting population and also because of the restrictions it makes. As to the additions: For many years I have expressed the belief that women of this country should have the vote. The women of England have been given the franchise, or the proposal is coming up soon. It is more or less limited,-but they are giving them votes. The opportunity comes at a time of necessity to give the women votes, and we are giving them votes in two cases. We are giving votes to the women who are serving at the front, and we now propose to give votes to the women who are kith and kin to the men who are serving at the front. No mistake will be made to give the vote to a portion of the women of our country. Great problems will have to be solved in Canada, as a result of this war, and nobody will have a better right to be consulted, as to the settlement of those problems, than the women of this country. They are in every way fitted to exercise the franchise, but it will take some time to settle the question of how the rights of all are to be guarded, as pointed out by the Prime Minister. But the great fact is that we are enfranchising a 'lot of women of this country. The matter is urgent, and has to be put through in a short time. We may not include all the women, but once it is started as it has been started in England, limiting it to those of thirty years of age and imposing other conditions, it will make progress in future. The provinces of Canada have given women votes in a number of cases. The likelihood is that the United States will have a federal franchise applicable to wo mein. They will isoon have it in Great Britain, and we are starting it now. No mistake is being made in giving votes to women.
I am in sympathy with the disfranchising of quite a number of people in this country. There is a good deal to be argued for the side of the case presented by the hon. gentlemen who preceded me. But, although it is true that we ought to give votes to those who become citizens of Canada, there may be times when necessity compels us to revise our attitude on that question. The hon. gentleman refers to Bethmann-Hollweg and men of his school. I may point out that because of the intrigues of these men, because of the necessity of our acting in self-defence, because of the ex igencies of the occasion, we have to limit this franchise as we propose to limit it

The ^national security, particularly when, it is in jeopardy, is a matter of supreme importance. The necessities of the occasion count for more than even the pledges we may have given in regard to political rights; as a war measure we may 'have to restrict rights that may have been conceded. Many people in 'this country, Liberals and Conservatives-I speak from no partisan point ox view-see the real national necessity of limiting the votes of these persons of alien enemy birth who have already got their citizenship. No great injustice will be done to them. Even though there may be an injustice, having regard to the knowledge we have of German and Austrian intrigues, I do not think that a great error will have been committed. I believe that the American republic, before their people come to vote, will insist upon some kind of federal law defining what shall constitute citizenship in the United States and stating to whom the vote shall be allowed. The Americans are having a great experience just now. They have not told us yet what revelations have been made to the President and his Cabinet at Washington concerning the ramifications of German intrigues. We are getting a taste of it now in the revelations that have been made in Great Britain. That being the case, the national safety demands that the franchise of these people shall be limited. Australia has taker, actum in this respect, not because of any hostility to the people who came there and helped them to settle the country, but for a national reason; for the safety and welfare of the Commonwealth. They are not denounced for doing that; neither should we be denounced for taking this action in a *case of supreme importance.
I have pointed out that we have been compelled to take this step as a war measure and because the Opposition saw fit to oppose the extension of the life of this Parliament. We had to pass the measure of conscription, having regard to our national needs; but the passing of two other measures, the one for giving the soldiers opportunity to vote and the other the provision for the regulation, extension and limitation of the franchise, would not have been necessary had an extension of the life of Parliament been made. Moreover, we would not have needed these two measures if Parliament had had what it ought to have-the right to regulate the length of its own life. I believe that Australia has that power; but we have not. One of the questions to be settled in this Parliament in the future will be the right of the Can-
[Mr. W. P. Maclean. 1
adian Parliament to regulate the length of a parliament. You cannot settle in a short time this question of citizenship; the question of to what extent a man shall be given the right to vote, the question of what limitation shall be attached to the franchise, having regard to the effect upon it of the operation of naturalization laws. Because necessity compels us to extend the franchise in some directions and to limit it in others, it does not follow that we are doing any injustice to a large number of the citizens of the country, but it does follow that we are doing something for the security of the nation and for the protection of the liberties of the people. You cannot take chances on a supreme issue of this kind; you must do what you think is right. This measure is a war measure; it is for war-election purposes. The Bill is justified, to my mind, 'and 1 think it certainly will be *suppoi'ted by the people whom I represent. I have no fear of the addition of a large number of women to the voting strength of this country. They will discharge their duty from thd highest ground of patriotism and from no partisan point of view. I am willing to leave the matter to them.
You talk about national unity in this country, and the necessity for it. How is national unity to be expected? National unity will be attained only if we observe some of the things that we have neglected hitherto. One of the first things necessary for the creation of national unity is a federal franchise. Sir John A. Macdonald was the first man who laid that principle down in Parliament. I often heard him speak on that point; from the first time I heard him I have believed in the principle, and I have asserted it in this House. I am ijather an old member now; I was in the House at the time we abandoned federal franchise and substituted the provincial franchise therefor. I never agreed with that course, and I do not agree with it yet; I believe in a federal franchise. Moreover, as I have said, I am confident that the American people will be compelled to adopt a federal franchise. Another thing that you must have in order to effect national unity-the Americans are coming to it-is federal enforcement of federal law. We run too much in this country in the direction of provincialism; we have to acquire more and more the nature of nationals.
We have to believe in the federal enforcement of federal laws. We have to become accustomed to look to the federal power for the defence of national and pub-

lie rights. We are now going through that experience. We are finding out that, in acting on the old lines that we followed for fifty years we were not acting quite in the right direction. We are retracing our steps and coming back to the views held by the old leader of the national policy in the old days. He believed also in a national franchise, and we are coming back to his view; and we shall make no mistake if we have a national franchise. We shall make no mistake if we enfranchise the women. We shall make no mistake if we declare that under the necessities that this war has imposed on us, we are going to revise and rewrite the law in regard to naturalisation. We have been too free in regard to our naturalisation law, and it must be rewritten. If there is anything that the war is teaching us to-day, it is this, that there must be a limitation in regard to naturalisation because of our experience of German and of Austrian ideas of integrity in connection with this war. We would have had no necessity for these two Acts at this session, if we had taken measures to extend the life of Parliament probably until the war was over. But,' that not having been done, the duty is imposed upon this Parliament to take steps upon the first opportunity to give this Parliament a power that the Australian Parliament has, and a power that we are fully competent to exercise, the power to settle in our own House how long Parliament ought to continue. We should not be cribbed, cabined and confined in that respect. We are a nation, and we are to-day that portion of the North American continent that is leading this continent in the defence of the great public rights that began to be recognized at the establishment of the commonwealth in England and that have come down through all these years. While for a time we may be charged with interfering with citizenship or with breaking a pledge, I do not think we are quite breaking a pledge. As a friend pointed out to me this afternoon, often when a man in this country is summoned to sit on the jury, a case will come up for-trial in which a friend of his happens to be the person to be tried. In such a case the court very properly says to that citizen:	You
must not try this case because you are an interested party. In this case we are saying to certain people of alien birth: Inasmuch as you are closely related to the man who is being tried here-and the Kaiser and all his works are to-day on trial because of his assaults on libertyyou must stand aside on this trial. We do not deprive that man of his rights, hut we say: On this occasion it is not fitting that you should be a juryman or a judge, and the citizen is the juryman or the judge to whom we are appealing in the coming election. While there -may be some ground: for the argument that has been made that: we are limiting the rights of people whom-we have invited to this -country, still if we are doing that, we aTe- not doing it because we want to deny them- their rights, so much as because we are determined to save the nation in this hour of its extreme peril. The women of this- country are, with us in this respect. Whether they will vote for us I cannot -s-ay, but I do say we are- making no mistake in recognizing the principle of "Votes for Wo-men." We are in this country recognizing the principle of public ownership, and now we are recognizing the right of the women of this country to vote. The women, certainly the women of my own province, will not resent the fact that the measure has not been made a broad one at the beginning. As was pointed out this afternoon, it will take time to- settle the extent of the women's vote, and we shall have to very carefully revise the laws of naturalisation. This measure, to my mind, is both a progressive one and one of necessity, and that being the case, I intend to vote for it and to justify my vote whenever I am called on to do eo outside of this House. I believe the majority of the people o-f this country are in favour of this law, not from any partisan point of view, but because of its fairness and because the necessities- of the war compel us to en-^ct i-t.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend (Mr. W. F. Maclean-) has promised us that if he is ever called upon, outside of this House, to justify the vote he proposes -giving o-n this- measure he will be able and prepared to do so. Certainly he did not this evening give any reasons in justification of his vote. Therefore, probably the- first opportunity he will have of making that justification will be outside of this Parliament. The substantial utterance he made this evening in support of this Bill was that national interests were in jeopardy unless this -measure was enacted. It would have better become that hon. gentleman had he attempted to give to this House his reasons for believing that national interests were in jeopardy. If national interests are in jeopardy, then probably this measure is justifiable, but when an hon. gentleman states that the
o536

justification of this measure is that national interests are in jeopardy, it is his duty to give to the House at least a few reasons as 'to why he believes that to be the case. He gives, as a reason in justification of his vote in favour of this measure, the fact that the life of Parliament was not extended. We very nearly had an election in the fall of 1914, and my hon. friend was then in favour of an election. In that event, there wag not and there could not have been a Franchise Act of this character. I remember reading the Sunday edition of a paper published by my hon. friend in the city of Toronto in the spring of 1915 to the effect that in a few days Parliament would be dissolved and there would be an election.
If there had been an election, it would not have done any harm.

In that event there would have been no opportunity to enact a measure of this kind. Therefore, in the two principal points my hon. friend attempted to make this evening in support of this measure, namely, that the national interests were in danger and that the Government was refused an extension of Parliament, he has signally failed in making good his statements. The Bill before the House proposes to disfranchise arbitrarily a portion of the people of this country. It proposes to enfranchise another section of our population who are defined in the Bill and who are principally relatives of those who have enlisted for service overseas. I have no difficulty in reaching a conclusion as to what should be my duty in the premises. This legislation is objectionable in principle, and I deny that there is anything in the world to justify its introduction or its enactment. Public sentiment in this country is not behind this legislation. There is practically no sentiment in favour of it to-day, and there will be less as time proceeds, I have reference to disfranchising clauses.
I submit that reason and justice clearly point out the duty of members of Parliament in connection with this Bill. A proper regard for the future of this country and for our good name among the nations and peoples of the world compel one to oppose the measure. It is not founded upon any principle of a substantial character, and I repeat what others have said, that it violates without cause an implied compact made between the State and a number of our citizens. It does violence to principles and traditions long established and long

cherished in all British countries. I believe it will be regarded as an act of injustice to-day, and that it will leave a legacy of distrust to a great number of people who will come into Canada in future years, which distrust will not easily be extinguished. Further, I believe it will perpetuate in the after-war politics of this country political incidents which should be forgotten. In our western country you will find one particular party, during political campaigns, appealing to the alien-born population for support upon the ground that another party during this war disfranchised aliens, and at the same time the other political party will be engaged in denying that allegation, which will be merely an encouragement to false testimony. Or if not doing that, they will be giving other reasons, and the result will be that many war incidents will be perpetuated. I believe, it is much better that they should end with the ending of the war. I maintain that history will adjudge the act contemplated by this Bill as a blot upon our national career. And, unfortunately, it comes at a time when we are writing glorious and imperishable pages of our history, which will be the future epics of this young nation. We have solicited to our shores the citizens whom wc now attempt to deprive of one of the rights of citizenship. In their native countries before	their	departure,	we	haveheralded	the	glories of	our	institutions.	These	immigrants	have	comehere, and no	one to-day	is	called
upon to defend them against any acts of sedition or treason or infidelity to their vows of citizenship. In this Western hemisphere, some day when the war is over, we will need more European settlers, as our economic future and salvation depends upon that. Many of the class whom we are now disfranchising by this Bill will be coming to this country, not directly from Europe, but from the United States, and I doubt if we shall not welcome them. Now I ask you, Sir, will this proposed Act fortify their faith in our political institutions? Is it worth while? Will it protect anything that is in danger to-day? What did my hon. friend from South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) mean when he said that national interests were in jeopardy?

If Germany succeeds where would our country be?
iMr. A. K. MACLEAN: Did he say what he meant, or did he mean what he said? We have heard members of the Government give reasons in support of this

legislation, and we have bad an opportunity of reading the Bill, and I say that in this Bill the Government do not mean what they say, or they do not say what they mean. It reminds me of the collision between two cross-eyed waiters in the dining room, which caused a downfall in china. One of the waiters said to the other, " Why don't you look where you're going," and the other replied, " Why don't you go where you're looking." If the Government meant to make this a war franchise based upon war services, they should have said 9 p.m. so in the Bill, and if they meant something else they should admit that they did not say what they meant.
The Solicitor General denied most violently this afternoon that there was any violation of an implied contract between the State and the citizen in disfranchising the citizen, and he referred to the fact that in the province of Manitoba Chinamen, though naturalized as British subjects, have never been given the franchise. I apprehend a distinction between that case and the one under discussion. In the one case the State has seen fit to withhold the franchise from a certain class of people but in the other case the State has seen fit to give the franchise. It is now proposed to take away the franchise from these people without showing cause. If the franchise is to be taken away from them, I say let cause be shown, and if it is impressive, if jt is substantial, just and right, then we upon this side of the House will acknowledge it.
To a large extent, this is a practical question. Let us see how many people it will affect. Will it affect such a large number of people that in the national interests their names should be removed from the franchise roll? If but a small number of the people will be affected, is it good business on the part of this country to enact it? If national interests are not involved and are not in jeopardy, by continuing the franchise to our alien-born, is this legislation really worth while? In that respect, therefore, this is a practical question. Now, how many foreign-born people are there in this country who will be affected by this measure? Some hon. gentlemen have already given the figures. I wish to repeat some of them, and I think it important that we should keep this in mind. In considering this Bill the people of Canada will naturally inquire, in the first instance, how many people of the enemy class there are 'in this country, and secondly, what is their	record as citizens during the
war.	In many	of the provinces
there is practically no German or Austrian
population. The foreign-born population of Nova Scotia is >about four per cent, and New Brunswick three per cent. Of the population of Prince Edward Island 99.4 is Canadian-born. The German and Austrian population of the province of Quebec is almost negligible. In the province of Ontario there is a large German population, the descendants, in the main, of settlers who came from Pennsylvania over one hundred years ago. In 1911, there were in the province of Ontario 7,871 German males over twenty-one years of age bom in Europe, of whom 5,143 were naturalized. There were 10,420 Austro-Hungarians of twenty-one years of age, of whom 1,049 were naturalized. In other words, the number in the province of Ontario is almost negligible, and that may be said of the province of British Columbia as well. It is in the three prairie provinces that we find the vast majority of alien enemy population. According to the figures given to the House on Saturday evening last by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. McCraney), there have come into the prairie provinces since 1900, 157,000 of the class we propose to disfranchise and he estimated that there would be about 30,000 of that class entitled to the franchise to-day. I think his estimate was about correct. According to the census, of 1911 there were in the prairie provinces 21,145 German males over 21 years of age, of whom 12,007 were naturalized. In the same provinces there were 57,750 Austro-Hungarians, of whom 23,846 were naturalized. This shows that in 1911 there were about 35,000 naturalized persons of the alien enemy class over 21 years of age in these provinces. There may have been additions since then, but on the other hand there would be subtractions to take .into consideration. Therefore, I consider the estimate given by the hon. member for Saskatoon to be substantially correct.
It is double now.

I doubt very much if it is double now, because the number naturalized since 1911 has been very small indeed. True, there would be a certain number, but I. deny the right of my hon. friend to say they have doubled.
I am speaking from knowledge of my own county, and I say they have doubled.

Canada is a little larger than the county represented by my hon. friend. In 1911 there were 12,007 Ger-

man males over 21 years of age naturalized in Canada. I doubt if the number has grown very much since. There would not be more (than 5,000 or 6,000 Germans who would be voters in the western provinces,' and I doubt if there would be as many as that. If that is correct, is it worth while violating so substantial a principle for the purpose of disfranchising that small number of electors, unless better cause can be shown for such an act. It must be remembered, also, that more than one-quarter of the German population in the Canadian Northwest came from the United States, a substantial number of whom were born in that country, and possibly their disfranchisement might be the cause of some international dispute, not of a serious nature, I grant you. I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce, is this legislation worth while, for the sake of disfranchising such a few Germans, who may possibly be very good citizens, and a great number of whom may be quite sympathetic towards the cause of the Allied powers? The Germans in tills country are different from the Germans in the British Isles, whom the Solicitor General says the British authorities deemed it not expedient to call upon for military service. Most of the Germans in this country came from the United States. The fact that they are settled upon the land and ciioose to come into this country to engage in an occupation of that character at once marks them ias a type of people different from those who went from Germany to secure occupations in Great Britain. It is well known that the racial affinities of much of the Austrian population, which is [DOT]the larger portion of the alien enemy population, are with the Russian people, and they are not known to be very sympathetic towards the Austrian Empire. If our political institutions were endangered by permitting these people to exercise the franchise, if these people of alien enemy origin were known to be hostile to Canada, to the British Empire and to the cause for which we now fight, if they showed acts of hostility in that direction; and if they were there ;n substantial numbers and so distributed that they could affect the result of an election in a number of constituencies, there might he something to be said in support of disfranchising them. It is not, however, necessary to defend them upon this score, because we have the favourable word of the Solicitor General upon this point. In introducing the Bill the other day, he said-
I am quite free to admit that taken all in all those who come from alien enemy countries have, in the main, during- the progress of the war, conducted themselves satisfactorily within lines of obedience to the laws of Canada.
And I thought he was rather apologetic in introducing the Bill. He did not unequivocally affirm his conviction as to the fairness of the Bill. He expressed himself in this way:
It does not seem unreasonable that they should not exercise, during the war, that control of our destinies which is vested in the franchise.
Those were not strong words; they did not indicate a strong and intense conviction in the merits of the Bill. He simply thought it was not unreasonable. I am told my 'time is up, and unfortunately I must come to a stop before covering the ground I expected to cover. I hope, however, at another stage of this Bill to have an op portuuity of concluding my remarks.

As I do not expect to be in the House when the vote is taken on this question, I would like to state my views in regard to the Bill now before the House. I voted for closure in regard to this measure, and on three or four occasions on Saturday night I voted against motions which I viewed as dilatory motions, only intended to retard the progress of the Bill, having *regard to the fact that we are coming towards the close of the session. I am a supporter of the principle of the Bill, and, if I stand alone on this side of the House, I shall so vote if I am here when the vote is taken upon the second reading. In my judgment, the matter practically comes down to three questions. First, is the proposal to give the next of kin of soldiers serving overseas, or who have served overseas, a correct one? After listening to a good many speeches here to-day, I have come to tlie conclusion that there is no very great difference of opinion on either side of the House upon this question.
There is a lot of difference.

If there is a lot, I have not heard it voiced during the course of this debate. I rather concluded from what I heard that there was almost a consensus of opinion in regard to allowing the female next of kin of the soldiers abroad to vote at the coming election. I do not believe that it will be possible to poll anything like the full soldiers' vote. I do not believe that you can poll the votes of men actively en-

gaged upon the firing line, of the votes of men who are prisoners of Germany, or the votes of hundreds of men who,are suffering pain and torment as the result of recently inflicted wounds

certainly you will not poll the votes of the thirty odd thousand men who have given their lives in this cause. For that reason, I am convinced that the proposal in this Bill to allow these men to be represented at the ensuing election is a proper one, and if it does not receive the support of both sides of the House, in my humble opinion it should receive it.
The next question raised by the Bill is that of disqualification. Upon this there seems to be rather a decided cleavage, those on your left taking the ground that it would be wrong, even as a war-time measure, to disfranchise men who have been granted the rights of citizenship in this country; And I agree that under ordinary conditions >
it would be nothing short of an outrage so to deprive them. But we must realise that we are not living under ordinary conditions, and extraordinary conditions require extraordinary measures. I have not had experience with what has been termed in this debate the alien vote which is resident in the Northwest. By that I mean that class of people who have within the last fifteen years come to Canada from enemy countries and who have become naturalized citizens of Canada. I do not know them nor do they know me. But I am going to talk perhaps a little more candidly about some former residents of Germany whom I do know; and I do not know that there is any necessity to mince words on. an occasion of this kind. I live in a county next to the county of Waterloo, and I believ-e from what I know and from what I have heard, and from what people in my -county know, that the foreign-born German population of the county of Waterloo are not in sympathy with the objects of the Allies in the present war. I do not believe that in my county there are more than fifteen ot twenty men who will he affected by the disfranchisement clause of this- Bill; but I believe there ate -a large number in the adjoining county of Waterloo who will be disfranchised. I will give an instance. I have held meetings in Waterloo during the course of the present war, several of them patriotic meetings, Red Cross meetings, enlistment meetings. One I have clearly in my mind. It was held in the riding of North Waterloo, at Elmira. There was an audience of about 300 people in the small hall, almost -all German either
by birth or descent, the majority no doubt Canadian-born. I made my plea on behalf of the Patriotic Fund. My reception was rather frigid, but perhaps I did not put the case as well as I might have put it. However, at the conclusion of the meeting, a gentleman on the platform came to ine and said: You must excuse us Mr. Guthrie, but take for instance myself; we are six brothers in my family, and five of us are in the Kaiser's- army, and, he said, where should my sympathies be? Well, it was a very pertinent question. I could tell from the -man's- manner where his sympathies were, and it was only human nature when you come down to the last analysis. I put the case to -myself-a Scotch-Canadian, suppose I were living in Germany to-day, unmolested by any law in Germany, where would my sympathies be? Entirely with the Allies. I believe that the highest responsibility cast on -any citizen of this or any country is the duty of defending his country, and the highest privilege which the citizen- can enjoy is the privilege of casting his fran-chis-e. On the one hand, you have the responsibility. But the aliens or the naturalized aliens in this country whom this Bill seeks to disfranchise are not permitted to defend- this country, even if they so desired. Whether it is a military regulation of the British Government I do- not know, hut I have been informed that men of enemy birth are not permitted to serve in the ranks of the allied armie-s.
Fifty have gone from Ottawa.

I believe some have gone from. Ottawa and some from my county, hut I can tell you of some who- went from Ottawa and my county, and that was the German reservists. My hon. friend says "not here." I have an instance, -and I know it is correct, because a brother of mine has- -been chaplain in an Ottawa regiment. A German prisoner brought in seriously wounded, when my brother was called to him, turned to my brother and said: "Hello, Dr. Guthrie; I used to go to your church in Ottawa." And that man told; my brother when he left Ottawa for the front. I believe there were a number of German reservists in Canada, and I believe that in m-any cases these were men who had taken the oath of allegiance to this country. We have had no serious outbreak in Canada-thank God for it-and I hope we m-ay not; but if one reads the United States papers day by day he will -see that the German people in that country have

been carrying out a most ingenious propaganda against the United States and in favour of Germany ever since the United States entered into the war. If that is so there, is it not likely to be so here? If the sympathy of the German residents of the United States is with the Central Powers, will the sympathy of the German people in this country not also be with the Central Powers? It is only human nature, and on that basis you have to deal with it. I do not believe that the men whom this Bill seeks to disfranchise will take serious offence in regard to it. I believe they will welcome it; I do not believe they want to be put in the delicate position of having to vote under the circumstances which affect them at the present time in Canada. No one believes this to be a permanent arrangement; this is purely and simply a war arrangement to avoid any difficulties which might arise, and for that reason I think it is proper that that portion of the Act should pass.
The only other point I see in the Bill is in regard to the women who are not enfranchised by this measure, certainly a very large number. I am a supporter of woman franchise for the whole of the Dominion of Canada, and I have not a doubt that, had there been time, that proposal might have been included in a Bill for the coming general election. But time has been otherwise occupied. We have been here month after month, and perhaps not a great deal has been accomplished; but certain it is that the House has been kept busy, aye very busy, early and late; and there has not been proper time to introduce general enfranchisement for the women of Canada. Five provinces, so far as their provincial affairs go, have placed Acts on their statute books to give women votes in provincial elections. Four provinces have not done so. Whether in these four provinces the great preponderance of opinion is against extending the franchise to women, I do not know. Certain it is .that the country is about divided, half and half, in regard to women's votes. I think that this question of the enfranchisement of the women of the whole-of Canada may well wait a year or two until matters of stern necessity with which we have now to deal have been successfully settled. I see no hardship in the Bill, no wrongful discrimination, and I have made up my mind to support it.

It is not my intention to deal with

the Bill generally. I wish to confine myself principally to the clause by which we disfranchise some half a million of the very best women in Canada. I would not ask that any one opposed to the Allies, such as Germans, Austrians or Bulgarians should have the right to vote in this country, but I claim that every honest, loyal citizen in Canada should have the right to vote. Why should we discriminate to that extent? I think it would be well to state to the House what the law of New Zealand is. The section reads:
Every adult person who has resided for one year in New Zealand and who has resided in the electoral district for which he claims to vote during- the three months immediately preceding his resignation on the roll of the district, and who is a British subject either by birth or naturalization, or a half-caste, is entitled (subject to the provisions of this Act) to be registered as an elector and to vote at the election of members of Parliament for that district.
Every man and woman in New Zealand 21 years of age, who is a loyal British subject, has the right to vote. In the small country of Finland there is only one Chamber consisting of 200 members. The system of voting is known as direct and proportional. The Finns have equal suffrage, and some 18 or 20 women are members of the House. I certainly welcome this Bill, in as far as it permits a large number of women to vote at the next general election, but it does not go far enough. It is narrow, it is drastic, and savours largely of kaiser-ism. I must take exception to the clause restricting and limiting the votes of women in Canada, and insist on that clause being amended, so as to give to all women who are truly loyal British subjects, if they choose, the right of voting. I say that a serious injustice will he perpetrated if the Bill becomes law as it stands. Why should there be any discrimination against one form of national service and other forms of service equally honourable, equally indis-pensible to the prosecution of the war? For the first time in this country, a Bill has been introduced which ignores workers for the Red Cross, and the win-the-war nurses, the different patriotic fund workers, Belgian relief workers, and tens of thousands of women engaged in the munition factories who will, under this measure be denied the right to vote. This Bill should be amended so as to confer equal political rights on women. We should give the loyal women of Canada the same political rights and privileges as are enjoyed by the men, with power to fill any office at the constitutional disposal of the Crown; and furthermore, to

Become candidates, and if elected to take their seats in this House of Commons. Then, and only then, -will the reforms so long advocated in this House by a numbef of the members become law. Penitenitary and prison reforms ably advocated by the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), reform in the liquor traffic by our good friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil), and last, but not least, abolishing of the death penalty in Canada. You are depriving of the vote by this Bill five hundred thousand truly loyal Canadian women, who have been doing all this good work ever since the war commenced. It is, to say the least of it, an autocratic, undignified measure and unworthy of any government of this great Dominion. I cannot understand how any government resort to such a subterfuge under the guise of a war-time election Act, and I hope that the right hon. leader of the Government (Sir Robert Borden) will accept my suggestion, and amend this clause. If he does not do so, I am sure he will regret it for years to come; and on the other hand, if he accepts my suggestion he will be able to look back upon this measure with pride, pleasure and satisfaction.
I must quote what President Wilson has just said in a message to the people of the state of Maine. It is an evidence that all over the civilized world Women are going to get the vote, and get it soon. He said:
May I not express through you my very great interest in the equal suffrage campaign in Maine? The pledges of my party are very distinct in favour of granting the suffrage to women by state action, and I would like to have the privilege of urging all Democrats to support a cause in which we all believe.
We are going very far away in this Bill from our democratic principle. I remember, in my young days, we used to say we were democratic-yes, "democrats to the hilt"-but there is nothing of a democratic nature in this Bill. The opinion of the people of Vancouver on this feature of the Bill is indicated by the following newspaper despatch:
Vancouver, September 7.-The Vancouver Trades and Labour Council last evening passed a motion protesting against the manner in) which the Dominion Government intends to extend a part franchise to women, and calling upon Premier Borden to give all women of the Dominion full privileges at the polls with men.
We have the following communication from Winnipeg:
Winnipeg, September 8.-"I am absolutely opposed to it," declared R. A. Rigg, secretary of the Trades and Labour Council, in referring to the new franchise legislation. "The country is falling into the grip of autocratic rule. The last semblance of democracy is vanishing. If
they continue along the lines they are now following, autocracy will undoubtedly be firmly established in this country."
In Montreal several associations have had meetings, and resolved on sending petitions to the Government and have passed resolutions opposing the Bill as it stands to-day. I will refer to one case. The People's Power League and Equal Suffrage League met last Thursday night, and the following is a report of the proceedings:
The resolution submitted by the Equal Suffrage League deprecated the idea of differentiating between one form of national service and other forms of service equally honourable and equally indispensable to a successful prosecution of the war, and that for the first time in this country a Bill has been introduced which ignores workers for the Red Crqss, Red Cross Nurses, Patriotic Fund Committees, Belgian and similar relief funds, also the tens of thousands of women engaged in munition factories, etc., who are denied the vote. It was also pointed out that many undesirable analogies will develop, and that it does not take advantage of the present psychological moment to confer upon women equal political rights with men, and that the British House of Commons and the United States have made no such distinctions in their recent franchise legislation.
It was, therefore, resolved, "That this meeting implores the advisers of the Crown to withdraw their Franchise Bill and draft immediately a measure that will invest women with the same political rights and privileges as are shared by men, with power to fill any office at the constitutional disposal of the Crown."
Here is one of the statements made at that meeting:
As regards the votes given to all female relatives of soldiers, nobody would grumble with that if adult suffrage for all women were established. But a slur is cast on every woman [DOT] who may be without soldier relatives, and she is declared unfit to exercise' the franchise! Why? What is the spedial reason for singling out a special class of women voters? It is not any frank recognition of woman suffrage, but as Mr. Meighen says, "to give added strength to the vote of the soldiers of Canada." Thus to 400,000 soldier votes will be added from half a million to a million soldiers' relatives' votes -a special class that no doubt the Conservative Government feel can be specially appealed to by being told the ridiculous rubbish that the soldiers at the front will be deserted if they do not all vote Conservative.
I appeal to the Government on behalf of these women who are doing so much good work. I will cite two concrete cases with a view to touching the heart of the Secretary of State, if I can.
It cannot be done.

I know a woman in Montreal with whom the Solicitor General also is very well acquainted. I have personal knowledge of the facts in this matter, because I have a son who is a major

in the 87th Grenadier Guards, a regiment which was raised by my hon. friend's cousin, General Meighen. The lady to whom I refer, who has no sons, gathered around her a number of workers in Montreal, and they sent 6,000 pairs of socks, all knitted by these loving hands, to that regiment. Is it fair to deny the vote to these women, who have been doing real service for the boys at the front, the sons of other mothers? I say that it is unjust, unreasonable, unpatriotic. In addition to the 6,000 pairs of socks, they sent over one hundred thousand soldiers' comforts of one kind or another. The Government did not pay for these; the ladies collected the money and sent the articles to the front. I submit that such women are entitled to the vote. Another woman had three daughters, and when the war broke out the very first thing ' she did was to say to them: come with me. Thereupon she and her daughters started working night and day collecting money for the Bed Cross and Patriotic Funds. Has that woman not a right to vote? I do hope that the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State will reconsider the drastic measure that they have submitted to the House, and will decide to treat all the loyal, earnest and patriotic women of Canada as they should be treated.

Mr. Speaker, we scarcely expected that this Bill would meet with the unanimous consent of members of the House. I have almost come to the conclusion that it is practically impossible for the Government to introduce any measure or to suggest any legislation that would be entirely satisfactory to the members of the Opposition. It hais been said that "only the dead are satisfied; they would not be if they were conscious of their dissatisfaction."
The hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat (Mr. Bickerdike), with other members of 'the Opposition, has paid great attention to the word "democracy," and has endeavoured to show by various means how in this measure democracy is being assailed. The very foundation of democracy requires that equal rights demand equal service. If we are seeking an exemplification of equal service as we should have it we shall not find it in the attitude of the Opposition during the whole course of this session; indeed, during the whole course of the war. The late Elbert Hubbard at one time defined democracy as follows:
1.	A form of government by popular ignorance.

2.	The fool's paradise.
3.	Any political system where male votes are a substitute for brains.
He had this further to say about the word democracy:
The word is from the word abracadabra; demo, lungs, and crazy; hence, to rule by caloric.
Democracy is defined in the Standard dictionary as follows:
The political system in which government is directly controlled by the people collectively through elected representatives.
Nicholas Murray Butler, in his work "True and False Democracy," defines both. He says :
Jealousy of power honestly gained and justly exercised, envy of attainment or possession are characteristic of the mob, not of the people; of a democracy which Is false, not of a democracy which is true. False democracy shouts every man down to the level of the average. True democracy cries all men up to the heights of their fullest capacity for service and achievement. The two sides are everlastingly, at war. The future of this nation as the future of the world is hound up with the hope of a true democracy that builds itself on liberty.
My hon. friend hag shown a. very keen interest in the unfortunate position of the women of our country, who, he says, as a result of this Bill, will be deprived of. the franchise. It was clearly shown this afternoon that what woman has never had she cannot lose. She has not had the franchise in this country go far-but I re-echo the sentiments that various hon. gentlemen have expressed: the franchise should be extended to women throughout the whole Dominion. The time will come when this privilege will be extended to all our women. How does woman view this measure? I have before me a copy of the London Free Press in which .are given interviews with several women. Amongst others, there is an interview with Mrs. Gordon Wright, a prominent leader in all social work, who is practically known internationally, and who has devoted a great deal of hex time and energies to women's work throughout the country. Mrs. Gordon Wright is the sister of Hon. Newton Wesley Rowell, leader of the Opposition in the provincial legislature. She was interviewed in reference to this measure, and this is her reply:
Mrs. Gordon Wright, sister of Mr. N. W. Rowell, leader of the Provincial Opposition, holds the strongest views on the subject, and considers that the proposals of Premier Borden are only just and reflect the greatest credit on the party.
"I think that it is perfectly right that only these women who have endured the anxiety of having soldier relatives at the front should

vote," she said, in reply to a question as to whether or not she considered that the Bill should he extended to all women, particularly such women as have no male relatives eligible for soldiers.
"X think that the Bill ought to go further and disfranchise all the men who ought to be at the front but who are not there. No slackers should be allowed to vote," she concluded.
Other women in the city were interviewed, and some of them expressed similar sentiments. Hon. gentlemen have said there is an object in this enfranchisement of women. Of course there is an object. That object is to do justice to the large vote of those soldiers who are at the front, and who will never have an-opportunity of exercising the franchise; and, as has been stated today, to do justice to the memory of those 30,000 soldiers who have made the last sacrifice, who are silent, who cannot express their views at this time, to the thousands of those unfortunate prisoners at present in Germany enduring hardships and trials, to the wounded, sick and suffering in the hospitals, not only in France and Great Britain but even in our own country, and to those who, by reason of the horrors of this war and the consequent strain on their nerves, have become insane, and who are now confined in hospitals for the insane in this country as well as in the Old Land. Do we not owe a tribute to the memory of those? Do we hot owe a duty to those who are still enduring hardships, who- will not 'be able in this election to exercise their personal influence? Should we not, therefore, endeavour to carry out the aims and objects for which they are fighting?. Hon. gentlemen opposite do not offer any serious objection to the granting of the franchise to the female relatives- of the soldiers, but they say: There is a purpose in not extending that franchise to the rest of the women. Certainly there is a purpose. It would be eminently unjust to those who have lent their sons to fight in defence of their country, to those who have male relatives at the front, if the benefit of the votes of the female relatives of soldiers should be neutralized'by the extension of the franchise to those women whose sympathies are not along the same lines. It is for this reason I can see a certain advantage in restricting the franchise at the * present time to those women who have relatives serving at the front. The Secretary of State (Mr. Meighen), in introducing this Bill, pointed out those who would be deprived of the exercise. of the franchise in this election. He said:
There are as well many thousands who are enlisted overseas, not in the Canadian overseas forces, but in the British forces. These men, though under the Military Voters' Act, they have, X understand, been given the right to vote, will inevitably in the main find it impossible to exercise that right. There are, besides, many thousands more who before the war were reservists in Canada-and some who were not reservists-who are to-day fighting in Europe or other continents the same battle in which we are engaged, but who are doing so as members of the Allied armies. They have not the -legal right to vote; if they had it, they could not possibly exercise the franchise. An election is to be held at a time when the most deserving, the bone, sinew and virility of our country, are only partially at least enabled to take part in the contest by way of voting. There are also thousands who have fallen in battle, whose voices are stilled. There are, besides these, some thousands who are prisoners of war. Their voices also are silent; under no imaginable circumstances could they take advantage of the Military Voters' Act.
Further oil he pointed out-and this was referred to by the Prime Minister this -afternoon:
Nor can we forget what is a more potent fact still; that each and all of the men overseas are stripped of the influence which under normal circumstances -they could exert among their
Hows in an election contest.
It has been painted out that, i-n so far as the alien vote is concerned, it affects more particularly those portions of Canada that we know as the western provinces. As has been showtn, -there -are some 12,007 German voters out of a total male population of 21,145 naturalised Germans, and that there are 23,846 Austro-Hungarian voters out of -a total male population of 57,750, or a total of 35,853 voters. If we had adopted the principle adopted by one of the western provinces, of classifying these men together and giving them three representatives, the same as they did with the -soldiers, they would not be -a great factor or influence in the politics -of this country or in this House. This Government is pursuing a wiser course, as I am more thoroughly -convinced after hearing the remarks of my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), who speaks from his knowledge and experience of the fact that alien enemy reservists, who had taken the oath of naturalization of this country, had responded to -the -call of their mother country and had returned in order to fight against our soldiers in the trenches. We have read the record in the press of a German who was taken prisoner, who was a Canadian citizen from one of the cities of Saskatchewan. He- was a naturalized British subject, a German who had taken the oath of allegiance

and who, to all intents and purposes, had accepted the conditions of nationality in this country. Yet he was taken prisoner from the German army at the front. We cannot get away from these facts which are presented to us. If there he one, if there be two, if there be a dozen, there is no reason why 'there may not be thousands of such men, and there is every reason to presume that those people of the same nationality, who were reservists and whose sympathies are naturally on the side of the country of their birth, would find that their affection for their native land was stronger than their affection for their .adopted country. Because we believe that, these men are not to be allowed to be conscripted into our army. Then upon what ground can these men who can give no service to the State in an emergency of this kind claim the right to vote under the extraordinary conditions which we have to face at the present time? My hon. friend has said that this is not a winrthe-war, but a win-the-election Bill. Personally, I do not see any great distinction, because winning the war, so far as Canada is concerned, means putting forth our maximum effort in order to bring the war to a successful conclusion, and I conceive that a government under the leadership of my right hon. friend who is now leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) would adopt a policy calculated to bring about results the very reverse of that.
I just wish to quote from the report of a meeting which was held in Calgary on May 17 last, at which Premier Sifton was one of the principal speakers :
Premier Sifton declared at the openingmeeting of the provincial election here last night that all subjects of alien birth who were naturalized before August 4, 1914, and who had In no way committed any offence against the laws of Canada since, would have the right to vote in the Alberta election.
There was a meeting of five or six thousand electors, many of them being soldiers who had returned from the front. Sergt.-Major Guill-foyle, one of the returned soldiers, was given ten minutes to address the meeting, and he at once asked the Premier why he had not taken action towards disfranchising all Germans and Austrians in the province. His question was the signal for shouting and applause among the soldiers in the audience.
The veterans claimed Canada was still in very real danger from these men, who were far more numerous than was generally believed, and who were now to have the right to vote.	.
The Premier, he said, had the opportunity during the last session of the Legislature to bring in a Bill disfranchising the Germans and Austrians, but he did not do so. Turning to the Premier on the platform, he said:	"I Sm-

peach you as failing to do the right thing for the country in this, and challenge you that you cannot make a reply that will be satisfactory to the citizens of this city."
Regarding the changing of the law affecting the franchise to subjects of alien birth, the premier said the proposal that this should he done was not made till it was too late for the legislature to take it up, and it was a matter with which only the legislature could deal.
I quote this to show that in that part of the country where the majority of these alien enemies are to be found, the soldiers who have lived side by side with them, and have therefore a better opportunity of judging them than we have here, find that they are not reliable.
I shall support this measure because 1 believe that its purpose is in the best interests of this country. Its purpose implies that Canada will continue with all her might and main to support our soldiers at the front till this wa-r is brought to a finish. I believe it would be a great injustice to the memory of those who have made the supreme sacrifice, if
10 p.m. those of alien birth in this country were allowed at this particular time to exercise the franchise and to ' use their influence while our men are engaged in the vital duties they are performing at the front.

There are quite a number of objectionable features in this Bill. As far as the question of -enfranchising the wives and daughters, and sisters of the soldiers is concerned,
I heartily support that particular provision of the Bill. I wish it had gone further and that the Parliament of Canada had enfranchised every woman who is, a British subject, following the lead which has been given in that direction by the western provinces.
The feature of the Bill to which I object most strongly is the disfranchisement of what- is called the alien enemy in this country. In the province from which I come, and in the constituency which I represent, there is a large number of so-called alien enemies, and from my knowledge of these people I take issue with any hon. gentleman on the other side of the House who states that these men are alien enemies in the strict sense of the word. I have watched their conduct ever since 1914; I have come in contact with them, and I say that in no act that I have ever seen has there been any justification for the charge that the Austrian and German in western Canada is disloyal. He certainly give? voice to no such utterances as I have heard in eastern Canada, and if the basis of this

franchise is- war service, I think a great many of the people in the eastern portion of Canada should be disfranchised before these so-called alien enemies in the West. We have tremendous natural resources in Canada; we have a wonderful country, which needs, above everything el-se, population. We have embarked upon a comprehensive scheme ' for inducing people to settle with us and become citizens. We have offered every inducement, and our policy had be-en successful up -to the beginning of this war. We have induced great numbers of people from all parts of Europe and the United States to come over and assist in making this a great country. We have given pledges -to these people that, provided they would settle among us and behave thems-elves-, Parliament would grant them the franchise and every other privilege a British citizen enjoys. That has been the secret of the splendid record of Great Britain as the most successful colonizing nation in -the world. Britain has never attempted coercion in -any country which she has conquered. She has never attempted coercion -against any people whom -she has induced to come and settle within her borders. From my knowledge of these people whom it is proposed to disfranchise, I know they hav-e been a very important factor in the upbuilding of this Dominion, and in the prosperity of the western part of the Dominion. They have proven most excellent -settlers, most peaceable neighbours, and a very honest, industrious and frugal people, who are transforming the country from a wild state into one of the most prosperous -and productive sections in the whole Dominion.
We have endeavoured to get these -men here on- the promise that if they came they should enjoy all the privileges which we give to- the native-born- Canadian or the native-born Britisher. And now, through no fault of theirs, with a stroke of the- pen, we are depriving them of this privilege. We are branding them in a way -as outcasts, and casting a reflection upon their loyalty, which, as some one remarked here this afternoon, will not be wiped out in- this generation, hut will probably be carried down for fifty years to come. From the point of view of unity, this is a most serious thing to do. In Western. Canada particularly, our population is necessarily of a very cosmopolitan character. We -are endeavouring by every means to unite the different nationalities into one common citizenship, and I take the view that we have succeeded
very well in my province. We have only one system of schools, and the German, the Ru-thenian, the Galician and the Pole has to send his children to our schools. They have to learn English, and, to give them only due credit, they are most excellent linguists. Within a very short time after arriving in the country they become quite proficient in the language. They are falling into our customs, they are doing as we do, they are dressing as we drees, and! they are assimilating themselves- in every way to the pattern of the Canadian people and are becoming excellent citizens. My hon. friend from East Middlesex (Mr. Glass) quoted an -article from a newspaper stating that Premier Sifton of Alberta had made a speech in CalgaTy which had not met with the reception it might have received from some returned soldiers in that city. I happen to know Sergeant Guillfoyle, who -spoke after Premier Sifton, and from my knowledge of *him I would not give credence to one word he said, no matter on what subject he wa6 speaking.
He was only willing to die, that is all. He offered to die.
A great many men offered to die-
But, he was in France.
-I am sorry to say my bon. friend from Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) was not one of them.

uniform on for a s-um-mer, and draw pay.
