I want to tell the House that those men responded splendidly to the appeal for contributions to the Patriotic Fund, and that the constituency of Whitford, represented in the provincial house by an Austrian, contributed more to the Patriotic Fund than any other constituency in the province of Alberta. Those men were most anxious to enlist. My hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) made the statement that one-half of the 218th Battalion was made up of men of Galician or Austrian birth. I have personal knowledge of the facts, and I think my h.on. friend is quite within the mark in that statement. To show the earnestness with which these men endeavoured to enlist, I might say they nearly all had to perjure themselves in order to become members of that battalion. They had to swear they were Russians, yet to my own knowledge the majority of those men never saw Russia, came from Austria. Still, they were so eager to go and fight against Austria that they enlisted claiming they came from Russia. The 192nd Battalion from the Crowsnest Pass, was largely made up of the same class of people, taken from the mines of Blairmore district, and that south-west country. So that the charge that these men were not prepared to do their duty and take the full responsibility of citizenship is absolutely unfounded. If they had been given an opportunity of enlisting and joining our forces under the volunteer system, we could easily have had a full battalion of men of that race.
I was much struck with a statement I read just recently, showing the feeling with which this question of blending and making a cosmopolitan community of blended people was viewed by no less a person than General Smuts, Speaking in London quite recently, he said:
We want to create a blend out of various nationalities. We want to create a new nation, and that is the South African nation. If we succeed in doing that we shall achieve a nation not standing on one leg, but on various legs. We shall have a nation which will embrace various traits. You will have a people all blending into one. It is only by bringing! about a union like that, and by mailing the different racial types of people work together, respect each other, co-operate with each other, and understand each other, that you will bring into being a unanimous people which will take the broadest and largest view of the problems with which it is confronted.
These sentiments breathe the spirit of broadness, and show that the idea of
[Mr. Douglas.!
cementing the people and nationalizing and colonizing is deep in the heart of that great Boer general, who not many years ago was fighting against Great Britain, and who today occupies one of the most responsible positions in South Africa. I understand the Prime Minister was at conference with this same general, and that those expressions were voiced at that conference, yet we find the Prime Minister coming back to Canada and at this late stage of the session bringing down a Bill which will have the very opposite effect to that voiced by General Smuts, an effect which will create discord and disunion in this country, >at a time when feeling is running high, when everything should be done to minimize differences and quiet people rather than the reverse. I regret very much that at this time of tremendous stress, when people's nerves are on edge, there is introduced into this Parliament a measure which is going to create such dissatisfaction and feeling, because of the fact- that an absolute injustice is being done to a large part of the population of this country.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the time at my disposal is very short. I must, in the first place, make complaint against the Government that this Bill was only two hours under discussion when the closure was applied. It is a Bill of far-reaching and great importance, and I think we should have been given at least a day in which to discuss it before the application of closure. Instead of that, one-half the members of this House had no opportunity to speak upon the Bill under the ordinary rules. We reached the discussion of the Bill at ten o'clock on Satuday night, and at a quarter 'to twelve the closure was applied. [ submit, therefore, that no great freedom or opportunity was given to the representatives of the people to deal with this most important question.
With you, Sir, I come from a province where the greatest possible freedom has been given to the people in connection with the exercise of the franchise, and where every opportunity is given to the electors or to any people entitled to he electors to have their names put upon the list; and the greatest possible hesitancy is exercised in depriving any of them of the right to the franchise, after their names have been placed upon the list. In the province of Nova Scotia we were accustomed to the amplest provisions for putting names on the list, and if necessary striking off the

names of those who had no right to vote. One has practically every day from the 20th of January to the 5th of March for putting names on and the same period for striking names off at the Revisers' Court, which is held annually on the 5th of March in each year; and if any person has reason to complain of the conduct of the revisers he has a right to appeal to the Sheriff's Court in each county, the provisions for that appeal being found in sections 25 to 23, both inclusive, of chapter 4 of the Revised Statutes of Nova Scotia, 1900. The revisers are appointed by the representatives of the people in the municipal councils of the different counties in the province, and are thus answerable to the public for their conduct, and are subject to penalties for any malfeasance of office as will appear from sections 39 to 42, both inclusive, of chapter 4 of the Revised Statutes of Nova Scotia, 1900. Subsection B of section 40 reads:
Every reviser who neglects to revise any of the lists of voters for the revisal section of which he is a reviser, or wilfully transmits to the clerk of the municipal district any incorrect list of voters, shall he liable to a penalty of two hundred dollars.	, f
Subsection (2) of section 40 provides that each day a list is delayed shall be a separate offence.
Section 41 provides that every sheriff who wilfully neglects any duty imposed on such sheriff by this chapter, or places on a list of voters the name of any person not properly qualified, or strikes off any such list the name of any person properly qualified, shall be liable to a penalty of two hundred dollars.
And although the Act, that is, the Franchise Act for Nova Scotia, does not provide imprisonment for any of those offences, yet the general law, as found in subsection B of section 48 of chapter 161 of the Revised Statutes of Nova Scotia, 1900, provides as follows:-
(b) That in default of payment of the said penalty, compensation, or sum of money, and costs, if any, forthwith or within a limited time, the defendant be imprisoned in the manner and for the time mentioned in the said statute or law, or for any period not exceeding three months, if the statute or law authorizing the conviotion or order does not specify imprisonment, or does not specify any term of imprisonment, unless the said sums with the like costs and expenses are sooner paid.
If these officers do not discharge their duty, they are subject to the serious fines, or to imprisonment. I find that the Act now before this House provides no such penalty, although the officers who are to
be appointed are not to be appointed directly by the Government or by any person who has responsibility for their actions.
I wish to point out, in the earlier part of my remarks, that the Naturalization Act of Canada gives very strong inducement for people coming into Canada to become naturalized. The provisions of our Naturalization Act afford ample protection to the foreigners who may become British subjects under the provisions of that Act. Section 24 of chapter 77, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906, reads as follows:-
An alien, to whom a certificate of naturalization is granted shall, within Canada, be entitled to all political and other rights, powers and privileges, and be subject to all obligations, to which a natural-born British subject is entitled or subject within Canada, with this qualification, that he shall not, when within the limits of the foreign state of which he was a subject previously to obtaining his certificate of naturaJlization, be deemed to be a British subject, unless he has ceased to be a subject of that state in pursuance of the laws thereof or in pursuance of a treaty or convention to that effect.
I read this to show that the Act which is now before the House does not propose to repeal this Naturalization Act, and the Naturalization Act gives to every man who comes into this country and qualifies for naturalization every privilege of a British subject. The contract is made with him by this House, by the Senate, and by the King, that when he comes here and is naturalized, he is, to all intents and purposes, the same as ourselves, and that right is secured to him by statute. The men whom we are dealing with here, so far as we have evidence, have done their duty, but we are not keeping our part of the contract. It is an old saying that " The subject who is truly loyal to the chief magistrate will neither advise nor submit to arbitrary measures." In this case also the old saying applies, that whatever we sow the same shall we reap. The Canadian people, in giving this party power, have sown the wind and they are. certainly, in this' particular Act, reaping the whirlwind. I submit that when we think of the practices and performances of the party now behind the Government and of the Government itself since 1911, we must not he surprised that we have this action of theirs and this Act before the House. When we recall, Sir, that in 1911, while the party of hon. gentlemen opposite professed to be super-loyal and were waving and flapping the flag and yelling loyalty all over the country, men of that great party were financing a paper and a speaker in the



province of Quebec who were not devoting much of their time to loyalty, we must not be very much surprised at what we find on this occasion.
We have been told by the Secretary of State that there was only one qualification for voters in this country and that the franchise could only be properly exercised by those giving service in the war. I submit that that statement is absolutely unconstitutional. In this country the powers and privileges of Parliament, and the functions which the representatives of the people are permitted to perform, are divided into two sections, one section to be dealt with by this Parliament, and the other by the local legislatures. The powers of the Dominion Parliament are set forth in section 91 of the British North America Act which reads:
It shall be lawful for the Queen, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons, to make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada, in relation to all matters not coming within the classes of subjects by this Act assigned exclusively to the Legislatures of the provinces ; and for greater certainty, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing terms of this section, it is hereby declared that (notwithstanding anything in this Act) the exclusive legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada extends to all matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated, that is to say:
The public debt and property; the regulation of trade and commerce; the raising of money by any mode or system of taxation; the borrowing of money on the public credit; postal service; the census and statistics ; militia, military and naval service and defence ; the fixing of and providing for the salaries and allowances of civil and other officers of the Government of Canada; beacons, buoys, lighthouses and Sable Island; navigation and shipping; quarantine and the establishment and maintenance of marine hospitals; sea coast and inland fisheries; ferries between a province and any British or foreign country, or between two provinces ; currency and coinage ; banking; incorporation of banks and the issue of paper money ; savings banks ; weights and measures ; bills of exchange and promissory notes ; interest ; legal tender; bankruptcy and insolvency; patents of inventions and discovery; copyrights ; Indians and lands reserved for the Indians ; naturalization and aliens; marriage and divorce; the criminal law, except the constitution of the courts of criminal jurisdiction, hut including the procedure in criminal matters ; the establishment, maintenance and management of penitentiaries; such classes of subjects as ar^ expressly excepted in the enumeration of the classes of subjects by this Act assigned exclusively to the Legislatures of the provinces.
Those are the many subjects which the people of this country are given the right to deal with by their representatives in this House. But we are told by the Solicitor
[Mr. McKenzie, j
General that all these subjects must be put to one side, and that the people of this country have nothing to say as to the class of representatives they will have to represent them, and they must only have men who give all their time and attention to questions of the war, and not to anything else. I submit that there is no justification as far as the Government is concerned, for introducing this new Act, and making these wide departures from the old condition of things that existed before the war or that existed up to the time that the Government received' the extension of one year. I submit to you, Sir, that, if this Government had declared to the people of Canada, when they asked for the extension of one year, that they were going to intro. duce a drastic measure like this, no sane man who had anything to say in granting that extension wouldhave consented to it but would have held them down to the proper procedure. H'ad that been done the people, before this date, would have had an opportunity of passing judgment upon the Government. We profess to be fighting for freedom. Indeed, we -are fighting for freedom, and for the establishment of the rights of the common people. Why, then, are we called upon to commit this very high act of tyranny, which is before this House? The proper rule is that, as far as the vote is concerned, there should he one vote for one man. That has been the practice in this country, and that is the practice in recent years in England, although there have been abuses of that principle for many years in that country. We depart from the traditions and principles of British institutions in disfranchising our fellow citizens and depriving them of the right and privileges which they have freely enjoyed. We are all for the war, for the King and for the flag. Where is the candidate going to be found from whom we have to expect any danger should he find his way into this House? The only danger that we have to protect ourselves against is that members may find their way info this House who will not be as true and as loyal to the subject with which we have to deal a>s ourselves. I have not heard a hint that any provision is to be made as to the class of candidate we shall have, and the blow is struck at the poor people, who should have the right to poll their votes in support of the institution which we are so proud to possess.
Why is there such fear about a change of membership in this House? The Government now have passed all the legislation

that they can possibly hope for. They have the War Measures Act, they have the War Profits Act, they have the Income Tax, the Soldiers' Vote Act, Conscription Act, Canadian Northern Act, the Quebec and Saguenay Act, the Overseas Militia Act, the Minister of Militia's Act, the Under Secretary of State's Act-every Act that the mind of man can think of they have 'within their power. I hope and believe that they have no part or parcel in the Acts of the Apostles. With all this machinery, -why fear to face the people? Let them give a proper vote, and allow the people to pass judgment on tlie conduct of this Government. We scorn, Sir, the political methods of the Turk ox the Mexican.	How ar^ they worse
than we are, if we follow the principle laid down in this Bill in our dealings with those who have come into our country and whom we have made British subjects.	If there is anything
wrong with the men in the West, or in other parts of Canada, who may exercise the franchise under the old conditions, we have no evidence of it. This Government has been delighted ter appoint commissions for every conceivable act that could possibly be thought of. They were always switching aside to some commission anything and everything that they should decide themselves. But here is one of the biggest issues that has been dealt with, or can be dealt with, by the Government-the question whether or not these people had the right to vote-and instead of sending a man to ascertain the true facts, or making any investigation, they simply pass judgment wit-n-out any evidence, condemn those men unheard, deprive them of their rights without giving them! the slightest hint? or reason a-to why the thing is being done, except that, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), it is thought they may vote Liberal. The soldier who fights for his country is doing his duty, and is doing it well, and he is certainly entitled to the first rank of citizenship. But he is not doing any more than his duty, and, as a citizen, as far as the vote is concerned, there is no law and there never was a law in any British country where a soldier or any citizen, no matter how admirable he may he, was given more than one vote. We have the foundation of the principle in our constitution, that the King can do no wrong. That fortunately is still true, but it is a sad thing to believe in this country the same cannot safely and truthfully be said of those who advise the King.

The Government promised those men full rights of citizenship if they came into this country, but the trouble is, sad to Telate, that those promises were ignored; and, as I have already stated, without the slightest notice and without the slightest opportunity of defending themselves the people are being deprived of that right.

I was going to say, certain emissaries went forth from this country to the West to ask certain gentleman to cast their lot- with this Government, -and come under the Tory yoke. But, -as they would not submit to the Tory yoke; as they would not come within the thraldom of Toryism, the next thing was to subject them to this law; to have them gagged, pilloried, outlawed. That is what is being dome by thi-s Bill. The Government says, sometimes boast-fuVy, that they are willing to submit themselves to the judgment of the people. Their courage in offering to submit themselves to the judgment of the people is -akin to that of the man who boasts of going into the lion's cage after he has had -all the lion's teeth -removed, his 61aw-s cut off, and his eyes gouged out. That is the courageous manner in which the Government proposes to go before the people. They say that they will win -the election; they boast -about it. Well, if they win it, it will he because of their having -seized their antagonist and tied his hands behind him. That is the extent of the courage iand bravery of hon. gentlemen opposite in offering -to -submit themselves -to the people -and in- -boasting of their expectation to secure the majority of the votes.
I warn the Government that in dealing with the foreigners as they propose under

this Bill, they are striki. g & blow at the principle of freedouj. Me ly of these men, when they came here, w re led to believe that British justice, Britis ; fair-play, British privileges, prevailed in tl is land, and that they woula have the advantages of all these. When it is known that tyranny rules, the stream of immigration into this country will be diverted to other channels. We have .heard a great deal of Canada becoming an adjunct of the United States. I submit that no stronger step could be taken than has been take- by the Government towards making this country an adjunct of some country in which freedom has not been flung to the winds. If an improper spirit develops in this country after this measure is passed, hon. gentlemen opposite will know what brought .about that condition, .and they will have themselves to blame. We boast of onr freedom, of our spirit of fair play, of our treatment of the people ,who come amongst us. Then why brand as cowards those people who come to our country at our invitation, to whom we have extended the right hand of fellowship, whom we have welcomed under the benign and munificent folds of the British flag? Shall we brand these people as men who are unworthy of confidence? I hope that it is not too late to save our good name, to stand steadily upon the rock-bottom principles of freedom, fortitude and fidelity, to be true .and firm for our God, our King and our country.
Mr. ARTHUR B. COPP (Westmorland): It will be admitted, Sir, that no legislation coming before Parliament is of deeper interest to the people than legislation dealing with their franchise. It is the duty of every citizen to go to the polls when the occasion demands and exercise the franchise which it is his privilege to enjoy. The people, therefore, are watching carefully and with a great deal of interest the Bill that is now before Parliament. This measure is composed of practically two parts; one, the disfranchisement of a certain number of electors; the other, the enfranchisement of a .certain portion of the population. The Secretary of State, when introducing this measure, stated that one of the purposes of the Bill w.as to disfranchise certain persons of alien enemy birth, practically all of whom resided in the western provinces. Personally' I have little if any knowledge of these people. I was particularly Impressed with the very careful, logical and thoughtful remarks made with regard to those people by the member for Sask-

atoon (Mr. McCraney). I am sure that nobody would charge that hon. gentleman with making a partisan speech on this subject; he spoke. as he felt. He referred to the people of that western country who -some many years ago, others not so long ago-took upon themselves the duties of Canadian citizenship. He said that they had conducted themselves as loyal and patriotic citizens during the whole of the time that they had been in this country, including the past three years, while the war had been in progress.
The Secretary of State said that one of the reasons why he introduced this measure was because a large portion of the population in the western provinces desired that they should be disfranchised in order that they might not have to vote in the forthcoming election. They stated, he said, that if they had the franchise some question might arise as to their loyalty. That was the only reason advanced by the Secretary of State for the disfranchisement of these people.' Well, any elector who feels that way can Tefrain from voting; it is not necessary to take from him the right to exercise the franchise.
My hon. friend says that this is a wartime measure; that the Act will operate only during the period of the war and the period of demobilization thereafter. But, however much we may regret it, we are forced to the conclusion that this is an election-time measure, not a war-time measure. Some'few weeks ago my hon. friend introduced a Bill for the extension cf the term of Parliament for another year. Seme hon. gentlemen on this side, as well as some on the other side, did not see eye to eye with the Government on the question of the further extension of Parliament, and because the resolution was not adopted unanimously the Government immediately started .to prepare for an election. A. Bill was then drafted and brought before the House, known as The Military Voters' Act, the purpose of which was to give to soldiers in Canada and overseas the right to vote. No one one this side of the House objected to the principle of giving to the soldiers who were fighting our battles every opportunity of casting their vote. I am sure that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) who had charge of the Bill will give at least some gentlemen on this side credit for assisting the passage of that Bill and endeavouring to make it as workable as possible.
A few days ago the hon. gentleman who introduced the measure now under con-

sideration was promoted to the higher position of Secretary of State. Certain newspapers supporting hon. gentlemen opposite expressed the view that his promotion was necessary in order that he might be enabled to look after the elections that were soon to be held. Well, he has started in very well to look after the election. The nekt Bill introduced was this one respecting the franchise, disfranchising in some cases and, enfranchising in others. I shall not take up the time of the House by discussing the disfranchisement of a certain class of the population. That part of the measure has been discussed very fully and very carefully by hon. gentlemen who have more information on the subject than I have. But I wish to refer briefly to the proposed enfranchisement of female relatives of soldiers who are at the front. I have never been a strong supporter of woman suffrage. I have never had objection to extending the franchise to the women of any province if I was convinced that the women in that province actually desired the franchise. I had some experience in the local legislature of my native province, and up to the time that I left that assembly and came here I had not been convinced that the majority of the women of New Brunswick actually desired the franchise.
I realize that there was a certain number who did. The legislature was waited upon by women from certain sections asking that the franchise be extended to the women, but I never felt convinced that the majority of the women desired that franchise, because in New Brunswick-and I presume the same is true of a number of other provinces-the women have a limited franchise in regard to municipal and civil elections, and very few of them, in those elections go to the polls and exercise that privilege. I do not believe they would show any more interest in casting their votes for provincial or Dominion representatives. But, so far as I am concerned, as soon as the women of the country desire that franchise, I am iprepared to give my assent to any franchise that may be extended to them. I realize as fully as any other man in the Dominion can realize the very great responsibility and burden that has been assumed by the women of Canada during the progress of this war, and I want to say, on behalf of those women who are not being given the privilege of the franchise under this Bill, that not only are they just as entitled to it as those who are receiving it under this measure, but it would be
in the interest of the women of Canada if the whole female population were given that privilege instead of only those who are related to the soldiers at the front. If you go into the rooms of such' associations as the Daughters of the Empire, the Red Cross or the Council of Women, you will find women working together, women who have worked together for three years in the interest of the soldiers at the front, and who are doing all they can in every way to give assistance and sustenance to our boys, and it does not seem right, just, equitable, fair or in the interest of British fair play, to say: We are going to give the vote to ten or twenty of those women out of one of those societies, who have been sitting around the table day in and day out-and almost, I believe, on the Sabbath, working for our soldiers,- and we are going to refuse to allow fifty others of those women to vote, l^ot only is that unfair, but it will have this effect. Instead of those women being drawn closer and closer together in the interest of the work in which they are so heartily and so sincerely engaged, a certain amount of dissatisfaction will be created amongst them, and the women who are not given the franchise will feel that they are not being accorded fair treatment by this Parliament in that regard.
I understand that, in some of the western provinces, if not in all of them, a list is made up by the enumerators as is provided for by this Bill. Therefore, they will not be subject to the same inconvenience that will arise in my province in which we have not that form of making up our lists. In New Brunswick we have always voted on the provincial lists. It was a very simple procedure, and a great deal of dissatisfaction will arise amongst the people of the different provinces who are not accustomed to these enumerators and this method of making up the lists. Very great care must be taken to ensure that a fair list is made up and an opportunity afforded to every person entitled to be placed upon that list to go before an enumerator, whoever he may be or wherever he may hold his court of revision, and that no unfair advantage is taken by any person for or on behalf of any particular candidate. The question of the franchise is a serious one in this country, one in which the people are very deeply interested, and one that cannot be passed over lightly or dealt with in a trifling way. It is a serious matter to interfere with that right of the citizens of this country, a right which they have enjoyed for so many years, a right which they will naturally
5612.

look forward to enjoy. Those of us who have had the misfortune to run many elections realize the dissatisfaction that is aroused in the mind of a voter when he comes to the poll and finds his name inadvertently loft off the list. He would sooner lose $100 than find when he comes to the poll that he has through inadvertence been disfranchised, and he will make more commotion, and more feeling will be aroused, over that one little thing than over other things far more important.
The Secretary of State told the House and the Country this afternoon that they were disfranchising a certain portion of the population of this country because he and the Government believed that those people would vote against the Government when it appealed to the country. He told us, on the other hand, he was enfranchising a certain other portion of the population composed of three or four hundred thousand women relatives of soldiers who had gone to the front, because he believed they would vote for the Government. So far as the rights of the citizens are concerned, it does not seem to me to be of very much importance whether they are to vote for the Government or against the Government. Personally I am not afraid to take my chance; I am willing to take a gambler's chance and trust my election or my defeat to the women who will be added to the list of the constituency of Westmorland. If we are to judge by the scores, the hundreds of letters that have come to me and to other members of the different constituencies through out this Dominion, from the mothers, wives and sisters of the soldiers who have gone to the front, who have had to wait month after month, and some of them over a year without receiving the fair treatment they deserve to receive and should receive at the hands of this Government which is responsible for the machinery for carrying on the different operations in connection with this war, the Secretary of State need not compliment himself too warmly or congratulate the Government too fervently in regard to the result of the votes of the women whom he has enfranchised throughout Canada on account of their being relatives of soldiers at the front.
In conclusion, I do hope and trust that the Secretary of State, who fathers this Bill, will see his way clear to extend the franchise not only to the female relatives of soldiers who have gone to the front, but to all women in the Dominion over twenty-one years of age who are British subjects. The women of this country are working

nobly and well for the Red 11 p.m. Gross, the Patriotic Fund, 'and other organizations for the comfort of the soldier, irrespective of whether they had husband, son, or brother at the front, because they realize that every man who has gone 'to the front and is fighting for King and country is just as much related to them in a national way as if he was their own brother, or husband, or son. I sincerely trust that the Government will reconsider that provision of the Bill and extend the franchise to all women of the Dominion within the limits I have mentioned, who amply deserve this consideration.

British subjects by naturalization-yes, provided that that naturalization confers upon them the status of British subjects throughout the world. Our Naturalization Act and the very statutes read here this evening confer upon the Austrians and the Germans in Western Canada "the status of British subjects only within Canada. They were not British subjects throughout the world. They were not British subjects in the United States. They are only British subjects in so far as Canada is concerned. We have just passed and placed upon the statute books of this country a Military Service Act, by which we have provided that we will take men compulsorily for the service of the State, and in so taking them the statute means taking them for the first line of Canadian defence in the trenches'of France and Flanders. Across the Atlantic, out of Canada beyond the three-mile limit, these naturalized persons cease to be British subjects. They .are not British subjects on the shores of France and Flanders. Therefore, at that moment, when they pass beyond the three-mile limit, that dormant alien nationality will revive, and they will again become Germans and Austrians. They are no longer Britons. Ceasing to be Britons, if they were taken prisoners in the front-line trenches, they would be shot as traitors, because they owed military allegiance to Germany and Austria. These men are disfranchised, therefore, by the law of their own country with respect to tins great war. Our law has declared whom we will take compulsorily to fight our battles overseas. The only men who can be taken-and we provide that when taken they are for that very reason given the franchise are our nationals. The minute these men cl alien birth pass beyond the three-mile limit their nationality revives, and once more they are citizens of their own state. But my hon. friends ask why they are not drafted into the armies overseas. I will tell 'you why. Because, under international law, no alien can be made to fight for the state in which he lives. Under international law Britain cannot take an Austrian or a German out of Canada, land him in France, and compel him to fight her battles. These men are aliens when they have passed beyond the three-mile limit, they are no longer Canadians, no longer British citizens, and under the canons of international law we cannot take them to fight our battles there. That is the reason why, under the Army Act of 1881, aliens are not permitted to fight 4n the forces of England except, I think, 
one in fifty. These men cannot fight, therefore, and so long as they remain in Canada they cannot be drafted by Germany or Austria; but onee they pass out of that limit, then, under the treaty powers, under our very Act of Naturalization, and under the Aot of the Imperial Parliament of 1870, which we copied, these men are no longer citizens of this State; they are Austrians and Germans; and as. such they cannot exercise their franchise in. this country. That is the story, and that is' the .reason why the great principle is being applied here that only nationals shall vote on national questions. And, nationals being only those men who are British by birth or naturalization-using the word "British" in the broad sense in which it is used in the new Naturalization Act which will be the enactment common to all the British Empire-these men. are not British subjects. As the great issue in this war is not only the life of this Dominion, but the life of the great Empire which we call the British Empire, and as nationals only must vote for the life or death of the Empire, it follows that these men, not being nationals, not being British subjects beyond the boundaries of Canada, may not, in Canada, exercise their franchise.
We have not rested at that, we have gone further. We have said that in this case where there is an obligation for military service, these men shall not be liable for that obligation unless they exercise the privilege of the franchise. ,On the one hand we deprive them of the franchise; on the other hand we release them from the obligation- the release from the obligation here, the deprivation of the franchise there; the release from obligation is part and parcel of international law. For this compulsory service they are required beyond the boundaries of Canada, and their latent nationality reviving they become aliens-Germans, Austrians-and as such they are deprived of the franchise because they cannot meet the obligation, not being British subjects in the broad and true sense in which that word is used. It is said that this is a political right and that under the certificate of naturalization they are entitled to all the political privileges that we are entitled to. That is true, and one of the political privileges that attaches to every man, if he be French Canadian, English, Irish or Scotch, it matters not, is that he may or may not have his name placed upon the register of voters. The same power in the legislature of Quebec

t
that deprived the officials of the federal Government of the vote in Quebec, that gave them a lesser status of citizenship, that deprived them in Nova Scotia of the vote under Mr. Fielding-that same power exercised in the federal domain is part and parcel of the political life of the country, and all that is meant, by the acceptance of political rights, privileges and powers under the Naturalization Act is that they accept what Parliament gives them in common with everyone else-nothing more or less. Any one who studies the statutes and studies history will find that that is the case. But there is another reason that it seems to me would be sufficient, if all other reasons failed, and that is that we in this country are at war and those who know, great historians and philosophers,'have told us that the tie of blood is the strongest of all. A great historian, some of whose writings I read the other day, said:
I put the motives of men thus, in order of their strength:
(1) Blood, that is race or nationality. (2) Patriotism or love of land and country. (3) Interest or the means by which man lives in trade and commerce. (4) Religion, which is the life and refectory of his soul but as a motive uncertain and incalculable in its influence, and (5) Politics, including all constitutional questions which are merely the means or instruments for attaining these ends.
So that blood ranks first in the motives influencing the minds of man. And I say to the hon. member for Strathcona (Mr. Douglas), notwithstanding what he has said, that there are hundreds of men who have left my province of Alberta, reservists for the Austrian and German armies, and hundreds remain there to-day who would go if they could-only the strong arm of the law prevents them from leaving for that purpose. To say that these men who would, if they could, use their rifles against our fellow Canadians shall have the right to vote against the man, one of the thirty thousand who died, is contrary to every principle of-
Hear, hear.

I say more that these men would be the first to say that is so. I have talked with some of them; I know something of their views, something of the opinions of these intelligent German reservists who have come to this country to make a home, and they tell me that the tie of blood is strong upon them, the call of the Fatherland, the call of the homeland, the call of brothers and fathers and cousins fighting in the German and Austrian armies. I talked to one the other day whose
uncle was an Austrian general. This man told me that the tie of blood is strong upon them; that they will keep quiet, that they will do nothing wrong, but will try and behave themselves-but the call, the insistent call of the blood is ever upon them. And these men should never be permitted to say whether or not our soldiers in the trenches are to be reinforced by their fel-law-Canadians. Such a condition must not, cannot be permitted to exist. Indeed, I believe that the great cry that will go up from the men and women of this country will be that this measure does not proceed far enough, that it will still permit some who are called by the call of the blood, the tie of kinship from overseas, to vote in this great election as the ties of kinship guide them and not as the call of patriotism to Canada should influence them. That is the story, and that is all there is to be said *about it.
1 heard the hon. member for Strathcona assail the word, the pledged word, of a sergeant-major who had gone from Calgary, a gentleman who went to the front and has returned wounded and retired from service. It ill becomes a man who all last summer wore the uniform of the Canadian Army Service Corps and drew the pay of his rank, to reflect upon that man who offered his life for this country. It is time that	sort	of thing	was
stopped, that that sort of arrant hypocrisy was no longer heard. I say by all the reasons that influence men's minds,_ by the influences that have swayed men in days gone by according to. all the great lawgivers from Uhe time of Moses even until to-day, those only who are nationals should decide our national existence and our national life or death. I know the men of whom I speak, and I do not blame them; I enter into their spirit; I think I know something of what they feel and how strong the call of their fellows is upon them, and that call, strong as it is, should be the cal] that deprives these aliens of the franchise in this country.
So far ias the enfranchisement of women is concerned, there is no man who will not say that the women of this country, by giving their husbands and fathers and sons in this great war, have earned the right to poll their vote on this great issue. No man will deny it. When you think of the long delays, the weary nights, the great anxiety, the teans, the strain that they have gone through while their loved ones have been at the front, who will deny them the right

to vote. And who, at the same time, will say that a broad and general provision of women's franchise should be enacted when a conflict of citizenship is upon us, when jarring and disturbing elements of nationality are on us, when fine distinctions that must be adjusted alike by the Imperial Parliament and parliaments overseas yet are unsettled-when all these vast problems are upon us, who would say that a general measure of enfranchisement of women should be given? Only those who desire to make a little political capital against their opponents.
But what of Canadian men and women, men who love their country more than their party, and women who place higher value upon the great sacredness of the ballot than upon the mere way of exercising it? They know, feel and believe that in a time like this there must be a dividing line somewhere and that dividing line has been found on the ground of personal sacrifice, thereby indicating that those who have given this service and made this sacrifice shall be those who exercise their franchise at this time. Let us not deceive ourselves. We are in the midst of the greatest of all conflicts. We struggle against spies in our own land. Spies have been discovered out in the western country. They have been found in western battalions, and have met their death as such in the early morn. There were reservists in the streets of Calgary a few weeks before the war broke out. They disappeared and are now prisoners of war with us. We are told of a German from Lethbridge being taken prisoner in .battle. Hundreds of men of that character were there. These men left our land after having lived amongst us and exercised their privileges as fellow citizens and are now shooting at our brothers .and relatives at the front. No member in this House should say that those men should have a vote, and men who would do the .same thing under similar circumstances, are not to be given the franchise. I will close what I have to say in the words of that great apostle, to whom my hon. ^friend from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) referred-" For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places.."

How desperate the
position of the Government is has not only been made plain by "the loud laugh that speaks the vacant mind," on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite who have just indulged in such unbecoming laughter, but also by the fact that-the Government for its defence has had to go outside its party ranks and call in, as its champion to defend this measure, an independent member who .sits on that side of the House. A little later in my observations I will refer to one or two things my hon. -and eloquent friend has said.
Synchronizing-as the Minister of Finance would say-with the application by the Government of closure to the second reading of this Bill, was the presence on the floor of this House this afternoon of Lord North-cliffe, the gentleman who led the intrigue that broke up the Liberal party in England, that deposed Mr. Asquith from the premiership of Great Britain, and placed Mr. Lloyd George at the head of a small tout select and powerful autocracy that sits outside Parliament, and which, as time goes on, deprives Parliament more and more of its hard-won- rights and privileges. Every student of reqent political history will recognize the, appropriateness of Lord North-eliffe's first visit to the Canadian Parliament coinciding with the occasion upon which the Government of the day resorted to the drastic measure of closure to force the second reading of the alleged Franchise Bill which is designed not to elicit an expression of the people's will but is deliberately designed to thwart the expression of the people's will. If the time at my disposal were not limited to 20 minutes, I might be tempted to indulge in a few observations as to the near or remote connection of Lord Northcliffe with certain recent political happenings in Canada, more particularly in the newspaper line. That, however much as I regret it, is an indulgence that I must postpone until another occasion.
Whether regard be had to the provisions of the Bill itself, or to the manner in which it has been introduced and forced upon the House, it is safe to say that the thought uppermost in the minds of the people of this country who are watching the despotic course of the Government is the one expressed in the old adage, "Whom the gods would destroy, they first make mad." On Thursday of last week, my hon. friend the Secretary of State (Mr. Meighen), in explaining this Bill, said that war service would be the basis of war franchise. In the very next Breath he made it clear

that war service is not to be the. basis of this war franchise, because the Billf while giving votes to the wives, widows, mothers, daughters and sisters of the soldiers overseas, denies the vote to the thousands, of Canadian women who. do not happen to have relatives overseas, tout who have rendered magnificent war service at home, in making munitions, in providing comforts and food for the soldiers, in Red Cross worlr. in Belgian relief work, and in the innumerable activities of the Daughters of the Empire, and of the Women's Canadian Clubs. All these women are to be denied the right to vote by this Government's Bill, although in five of the provinces they have such right under the Provincial Franchise Act, which this Bill adopts, but only after it strikes off the names of those women who otherwise would have their franchise preserved. This point cannot be made too clear. For the purpose of emphasizing it, let me refer to a question and answer reported in the proceedings of this House of September 6th, 1917, at page 5729 of Hansard.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier:	Am I right in this:
that while the women of Ontario and the western provinces have to-day, under the laws of those provinces, the right to vote, they will, with the exception of those who are qualified as the relatives of men who have enlisted, not have the right to vote in this election?
Mr. Meighen:	That is correct.
In view of this statement, in justice to the thousands of Canadian women who have rendered war service of incalculable value, how hollow is the pretense of my hon. friend the Secretary of State when he said that this Bill was an attempt on the part of the Government to repair an injustice. This Bill repairs no injustice; it does actual injustice to thousands of loyal, law-abiding Canadians, of whom the women I have mentioned are only one class.
Let us consider another class for a few minutes.. It has toeen stated over and over again in this country, and by none more loudly than by hon.. gentlemen opposite and their supporters through the country, that Canada's participation in this war is against the Kaiser and kaiserism, and not against the German people.
But, Sir, this Bill is directed not against the Kaiser and kaiserism, but against the German people themselves, who are resident within the boundaries of Canada. Once this game of disfranchising the foreigner whom we bring 'to our shores and to whom we guaranteed equal citizenship 'and equal rights with ourselves - is begun, where, I ask you, is it likely to stop? A moment's reflection will show how vicious is the step
which the Government is taking in this Bill. As you are quite well aware, the Allies of to-day may be the enemies of tomorrow; all history proves that. To-day we propose in this Bill to disfranchise the Germans, Austrians, Hungarians and Bulgarians in Canada because they are of enemy country origin. If in the next war Belgium, Russia, Italy, Sweden, Norway and the United States are opposed to Great Britain, then to be consistent we will, in the case of a war-time election, have to disfranchise all the Belgians, Russians, Italians, Swedes, Norwegians and Americans within our borders. It is quite obvious, therefore, that by introducing this measure the Government has at one stroke succeeded in embittering our foreign-born citizens whom we now propose to disfranchise, land lin implanting suspicion .and distrust in the minds of those other citizens whose turn may come next.
The member for Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett), in his eloquent address of a few minutes ago, said that in the discussion of this question it was absolutely necessary to keep separate the questions of franchise and citizenship. I accede to that suggestion, but I want to point out that that does nott extricate the Government from the difficulty into which it has got' itself by introducing this Bill. Neither, I submit, does my hon. friend's reference to the disfranchising of certain oiviil servants in. .the province of Quebec by the provincial Government help this Government Sue iota in connection with this measure. That has nothing to do, for instance, with the case of the Mennonites, who aTe .affected by the BUI before the House, in 1873 ox 1874 we 'entered into a .solemn treaty with those people. We brought them to Canada under the express provision, in what they rightly claim to be their bill of rights, that they were to have the use of their language and to be exempt from military service. In the original Bill of rights they were guaranteed the other right of citizenship, that of the franchise, when they should become naturalized. In the Bill before us we tell these people that if they exercise the franchise they are not exempt from military service, and to that extent we break faith with those whom we brought to Canada under the solemn compact entered into in 1873 or 1874. My hon. friend's argument in reference to citizenship and to franchise, so far as he proposes to apply it to certain residents of the western provinces, is refuted by the fact that the 218th Battalion, which was raised

and sent to the front from my hon. friend's province, was, I am told, composed in large part of Austrians whose services this Government was glad to accept.
On Saturday last two notable speeches were delivered in this discussion., one by the member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) and the other by the member for Saskatoon (Mr. McCraney). They told how this Bill would affect certain groups of citizens in the western provinces from which they come; their speeches were most interesting .and most illuminating.
Let me illustrate for a few minutes how this Bill affects another group of citizens who reside here in Ottawa. I am informed that there are about 1,500 Germans in this city and that several families among them settled here nearly fifty years ago. In times past many of these men joined local regiments here, notably the .Governor General's Foot Guards, the 43rd Regiment, and the Ottawa Field Battery. It appears that these Germans were told that the oath of allegiance which they took on joining these units gave them the right of citizenship. In any event, they exercised these rights for years without question or hindrance. In more recent years, however, these men discovered that they had been misled, and the majority, I am told, have been naturalized within the last fifteen years. These men, with the exception of those who have sons, grandsons or brothers overseas fighting in the ranks of the Allies, will be disfranchised by the measure which is now before the House. Naturally, that will raise feelings of deep resentment in the breasts of these men, all the deeper in view of their conduct since the beginning of the war. In the first year of the war an agitation based on ignorance was started against these people in Ottawa. It was about the time of the sinking of the Lusitania, and some of the agitation centered around that tragic event. But these Germans, while law-abiding people, are not inclined to lie down under an injury. They held a public meeting under the auspices of the St. Paul's German Lutheran church in this city, and they passed a resolution which I shall take the liberty of reading to the House. As published in the papers of May 18, 1915, that resolution was as follows:
Whereas members of this congregation have been resident in Ottawa and vicinity for nearly half a century and it is now more than forty-one years since they built their first church for divine worship at the corner of King Edward avenue and Wilbrod street in this city;
[Air. Murphy.]
And whereas during the whole period of their residence in this city the members of this congregation have lived on terms of amity and good will with their fellow-oitizens and are sincerely desirous that these amicable relations should continue to exist;
And whereas certain false statements designed to prejudice the members of this congregation in the eyes of their fellow-citizens have lately been published with reference to certain events of the present deplorable war, and it is deemed advisable to refute these statements by unanimous and official action on the part of the congregation ;
Now, therefore, be it resolved as follows:
That as Canadians and British subjects by birth or naturalization, we recognize and profess no other loyalty than that which we cheerfully render to Canada and the British Empire;
That as citizens we claim the right to share at all times in the trials and sacrifices of this Dominion, and, having regard to our numbers and financial means, we have willingly assumed our share of the burden which such a right imposes in the present struggle against the demon of militarism ;
That we condemn as a deliberate and inhuman crime the sinking of the Lusitania and the employment by the Germans of other methods of warfare which are equally unjustifiable ;
That we deplore the great loss of life entailed by the employment of such un-Christian methods, and we pledge ourselves anew to further assist Canada and the Empire in the task of destroying the military autocracy which has so long menaced the peace of the world;
And be it further resolved that copies of these resolutions be sent to His Worship Mayor N. D. Porter and to the city newspapers.
Signed by the vestry on behalf of the congregation,
Aug. Garske,
Fred. Kritsch,
Robt. A. W. Hupp.

That is not all. My further information is that approximately fifty of these men enlisted and went overseas; that four have been killed in action; that two have died of wounds; that 'several others have enlisted and were later discharged as medically unfit. I am told also that no class of our citizens have contributed more frequently and more generously to patriotic and charitable objects connected with the war than this same group of German Canadians. It is natural that the men of this group who are to be disfranchised should be incensed against the Government. They ask: If onr vote is to be taken away, if we are to be denied a voice in saying how and by whom Canada's participation in this war shall be conducted, then will the Government, after the war is over, also exempt us from taxation levied on account of the war? That is a question this Government will have to answer, and that is only one of the many different questions they will

have to answer because of the introduction of the measure now before the House.
If this Bill is unjust in many respects, it is ludicrous in some others. Let me cite one of the latter kind. Section 3 of the Bill provides that:
Any deputy returning officer, either of his own motion or at the request of any agem or scrutineer, after carefully explaining the meaning of paragraphs (g) and (h) of section 67 of this Act

His manner?

Would they not exercise the franchise as intelligently as those who have relatives at the front? This measure is discriminatory. It is not fair. It is not a British measure. The Prime Minister and the Secretary of State have told us that in this measure the Government is adopting the provincial franchise. That statement is not entirely correct, because in five of the provinces the franchise has been given to women by the provincial legislatures, irrespective of whether they have relatives at the front or not, whereas this measure restricts it to women who have relatives at the front. This measure also departs from the provincial franchise in the preparation of the lists. According to our electoral law, we use the provincial lists, which are made by the municipal officers who are impartial and1 independent of party politics. By 'this measure the lists made by the municipal officers are to be only partially adopted. The lists will be partly made by enumerators who will he appointed by the Government who will be partisans of the Government and who will have large



discretionary powers. They may refuse to place men on the lists on the pretext that they are aliens, or that their mother tongue may be alien, whereas the main reason for leaving them off is that these enumerators may suspect they will cast their votes for the Liberal candidate.
They have an appeal, have they not?

There is no appeal. There are appeals in regard to the lists made in cities and county and district towns of over 9,000 population, but in the other municipalities, which are in ihe majority, there is no appeal. The list made by the enumerator will be final, although, if a man is not on the list, he can go to the polling booth and cast his vote if he is prepared to swear he was omitted from the list and has the right to vote. You know, Mr. Speaker, that persons who are not. on the list would not care to go through the ordeal of taking an oath in order to be entitled to cast their votes. In any event, even if they do vote, it does not count until it is established before the judge that they had the right to vote. It is only on a recount that these votes would be counted. Austrians, Germans, and others from enemy countries or whose mother tongue is that of an enemy country may have come here years ago. They came at the invitation of the Government. They have settled in our Northwest, they have cultivated the land and developed the country, they have taker their naturalization papers and have beer, assured that they will be granted the privileges of British citizenship. These people have not been guilty of any sedition or disloyalty. If they were, certainly this Parliament would have the right, and would have more than the right, the duty, to deprive them of the franchise.
I was surprised to hear the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) say that the Germans of Ontario, as a rule, were disloyal. I think that my hon. friend has exaggerated the situation. There may be a few who are disloyal. But if he got a frigid reception at one patriotic meeting, that does not say that they are disloyal or guilty of sedition. We say that blood is thicker than water. Their blood is not British blood or French blood; their blood is the blood of people who are at war with France and England. The hon. member cited one particular instance, but we must not judge a whole nationality by one instance.
Besides depriving those people of their franchise, I maintain that this Act is going

to create disunion and discord in this country. Even the people who are not deprived of their franchise, because they were naturalized before 1902, will resent the insult which is offered to them by this measure. This is a disrupting measure. May I quote, to substantiate my statement, an article which appeared in the Toronto Globe of last Saturday. The Toronto Globe is not very partial to the Liberal party. For some time it has favoured the Government rather than the Opposition. It has supported the Government very strongly on the Military Service Bill and other measures since the beginning of the session. The Globe saysr-
A Disruptive Measure.
The War-Time Election Act is a surrender on the part of the Government to the machine element of the party. It strengthens the suspicion that manipulation of the franchise is a punishment for those western Liberals who refused to enter a National Government under the leadership of Sir Robert Borden. It is asserted that when the western men were in Ottawa the Prime Minister told them that any Act of disfranchisement would be personally repugnant to him. But, as in many other instances, he has been too weak to withstand the pressure from certain of his colleagues.
As a practical means of winning a Federal election the Act is futile and clumsy. The last census showed that the proportion of Canada's voting population designated as "foreign-born" was only 6.62 per cent in 1911. The influx of settlers into the country since then, and the efflux of English-speaking men during the past three years of war, possibly may have increased that proportion to ten per cent, and only a portion of this number is of enemy origin. For the sake of eliminating a fraction of the total vote the Government would inflict a gross injustice on law-abiding members of the community.
The Act proposes to disfranchise two classes of people in Canada. All conscientious objectors to the war would be prevented from voting at the next general election, and all citizens of alien enemy birth or near extraction. That means that German Mennonites and the Douk-hobors would be ruled out in the first class, and probably the members of the Society of Friends, whose loyalty has never been questioned, and that all the Ruthenians, Austrians, Hungarians, and Germans who live in the northerly districts of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba would largely compose the second class.
Few of the German population of the West have come directly from Germany to Canada. The majority of them have been classed among the immigrants who have crossed over the line from the United States. One-third of the so-called American settlers in the West are of Teutonic origin. Many of them, although born in Austria or Germany had become thoroughly Americanized before coming to this country, but they are disfranchised in the present Bill.
At no time since the war began have the Austrian or German people of the West given the authorities any trouble. The very act of disfranchising those foreigners who have been naturalized, especially the Ruthenians, who have entered most generally into the political

life of the West, will tend to solidify them, and even arouse hostility towards constituted authority. This Act will make enemies out of thousands of men and women who have become Canadians in spirit and outlook. The mere loss of their ballots will not mean much to one political party or the other, but the enactment of a hostile law by the Government of Canada, which made a contract of citizenship with them when they entered the country, will create a potential animosity which the Dominion can ill-aiford to invite.
The Dominion Government has thrust the responsibility of making Canadians out of the new peoples from other countries upon the provinces. In the case of the young provinces of the West that duty has been particularly onefous during the past twelve years. Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba were confronted with the problem of assimilating the hordes of new settlers which descended upon them between the years 1902 and 1914. The coming of the war stopped the influx of new citizens from Europe, and made a breathing spell in which the West was able to recover itself from the rush of immigration days. The schools, colleges and universities of the West have done great work in meeting the urgent national demand for education. On the other hand, the different nationalities from Europe have had a beneficial effect upon the life of the western plains. Professor W. C. Murray of the University of Saskatchewan, in an address at Saskatoon two years ago, said:	'The life of this
province is being greatly enriched by the artistic, literary and musical gifts which they and their people are bringing to us. We of Canadian birth do not realize to the full how much Saskatchewan owes to European culture. Every musical festival, each convention, be it grain growers, homemakers or municipalities, but deepens the conviction that their high character is due to the training and culture of Britain and the continent of Europe." Interference at this time with the important process of assimilation, which is being directed so conscientiously by the educationists of the western provinces, will do untold injury to the life of the whole Dominion.
The proposed disfranchisement Act is also a breach with the best traditions of the British Empire. Let the politicians at Ottawa take thedr cue on this question from that great patriot. General Smuts, whose speeches stirred London so deeply last spring. Speaking on the future of South Africa, he set down the soundest of Imperial principles when he said: "We want to create a blend out of various nationalities. We want- to create a new nation, and that is the South African nation. If we succeed in doing that we shall achieve a nation not standing on one leg, but on various legs. We shall have a nation which will embrace various traits. You will have a people all blending into one. It is only by bringing about a union like that, and by making the different racial types of people work together, respect each other, co-operate with each other, and understand each other, that you will bring into being a unanimous people which will take the broadest and largest view of the problems with which it is confronted."
In this fiftieth anniversary of Confederation it would be a poor monument indeed to place among the laws of Canada, one which would be calculated to subvert rather than perpetuate the idea of a Canadian nationality.
