1 submit that the character of this measure cannot be better characterized than by this article of the Globe. This Bill also deprives the conscientious objectors of the right to vote. These people, Mennonites .and Dukhobors, came here on the invitation of the Government. They had objections to military service, and left their countries ot origin on account of military service, and they were granted this privilege by Orders in Council .passed by the Government in 1873 and 1898. And now this Government wants to break faith with these people ami to deprive them of their vote. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) does not seem to take great interest in this measure; he seems to have left it entirely in the charge of the Secretary of State (Mr. Meighen), which leads me to believe that this measure is brought into this House for the purpose of wresting the West from the Liberal party, and preventing a majority of Liberal members from being elected in the western provinces. The Government know that if they want to stay in power they must get a majority in the West. They know that Quebec will give a strong majority for the Liberal party, as Ontario may give a strong majority for the Conservative party, that the Maritime Provinces together may give a majority to the Liberal party, and if the Government want to stay in power they must certainly get a majority in the western provinces. The larger number of aliens reside in those provinces, and the Government wants to prevent those people from voting for the Liberals, as a large number of them have done in the past. Those people have not been guilty of any sedition or disloyalty, and some of them, according to the statements of my hon. friend from Saskatoon (Mr. McCraney) and my hon. friend from Strathcona (Mr. Douglas) contributed largely to the Patriotic Fund, some of their sons have gone to the front, and some have offered, their 'services, but have been refused. A great many of these people, Galicians, Ruthenians and Bukowinians, are Slavs and are not of Teutonic origin. Their sympathies are with Russia and the Allies in this war, rather than with the Central Powers.
Although only a few in my constituency will be deprived of their votes, I thought it was my duty to protest. Even if one of my constituents were deprived of his vote, I would be lacking in my duty if I did not rise and protest against the measure, which I can only Characterize as un-British. There

was a war in South Africa seventeen years ago, and this country sent seven or 'eight thousand soldiers to that country, and spent half ia million dollars to vindicate for the British subjects in South Africa the right to exercise their franchise. When the Government of the Transvaal wanted to deprive the British subjects who had resided there for twenty years of theiir right to vote, England declared war against the President of the Transvaal, ;and the colonies came to the rescue. England spent hundreds of millions of dollars, and many thousands of British soldiers died on the field of battle, and some hundreds of Canadian soldiers lost their lives, only to vindicate the right of British subjects to exercise the franchise. Now they want to disfranchise citizens who came here fifteen years ago, who have been loyal to the British flag, and it is only for one purpose-to get them back into power.

Since the stirring incidents of Saturday evening, I have had occasion to read over in French and English the Bill which is at present before the House, and the principle of which we are discussing upon the second reading. I have searched in that Bill to find a good point, and have heen>
unable to find any. I find that the Bill as drafted is an insult to British loyalty, and to the great majority of the people of Canada. First, it is an insult to the majority of the people of Canada because this Government, in introducing this Bill, brands a certain portion of our population as absolutely disloyal to the Crown: they have served faithfully and well for the past 15 years. The Secretary of State, in introducing the Bill at page 5725 of the Unrevised' Hansard said, speaking at that time of the aliens who are naturalized citizens of Canada, and who are being deprived- of their vote:
Not only is it unfair to them that they should be asked to decide the destiny and the vigour of a war against their brothers in Europe,' but it is unfair to the rest of the papulation that they should have the right to so decide.
How could they, by their vote, decide the vigour of the war which is being waged against their brothers, unless, Mr. Speaker, that statement means that in voting for a Liberal candidate and the Liberal party they will be doing less for the British Empire and for the war than if they voted' for our good friends on the other side of the House? What right has the Secretary of State, or any man in this House, to brand the Liberal party as disloyal? Have not our members on this side of the House given

just as freely and just as willingly of their eons, and of their flesh and blood, to the defence of the Empire?
No?

Have not the Liberals from one end of Canada to the other enlisted just as freely as the Conservatives? Do hon. members on the other side contend that the Conservatives are the only people who have enlisted in this war? The difference between the two parties i-s this; that if the Liberal party is returned to power during the coming election, the war will be continued as it has been waged since the beginning. The soldiers of Canada will be members of a volunteer army fighting with vigour and enthusiasm, hoys who are willing to fight for their King and country, and if the Conservative party is returned to power, what shall we see? We shall see a conscript army where you will have to be prodding the soldier in the .back with a sword to make him fight. That is the difference between the two parties. The policy of the Liberal party has 'been laid down and published in the press of this country, under the signature of my right hon. leader Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who tells us, not that he wishes to relax in any way the part that Canada is taking in this war, but that he desires to consult the Mother Country, and to apply the energies of Canada in the way which will do the most good to the Mother Country. He promises a vigourous recruiting campaign, and he assures the people of Canada and of the Empire at large that Canada will maintain her position in this war as a free and autonomous colony of the British Empire. The Liberals cannot be branded as disloyal. They have contributed generously to the Patriotic Fund, to all the different relief funds which have been working throughout the country, and it is from the Liberal side of this House that the statement has been made, and that motions have been made which have been turned down by the other side, that the people of Canada, as .a whole, and the Government of Canada should not rely on public charity to look after the welfare of the wives aand children of soldiers who are fighting for us on the other side of the ocean, but that this patriotic duty should be performed by the Government itself. I feared that I misunderstood the Secretary of State, and I kept on reading his remarks.
I find the following words a few lines further down.
It is because of the reasons I have mentioned, namely, that those who cannot in the nature of things be absolutely divorced in sym-

pathy or sentiment from the peoples from whom they come should not be permitted, in justice to the rest of the population, to exercise a measure of control over the destinies of the war against those p'eoples, because it would be unfair to them to ask them to go to the polls and vote on an issue which decides to a degree the vigour, the purpose and the destiny of that war.
I dissent emphatically from that statement. I find coupled with that another statement, as follows:
It is also because war service should he the basis of war franchise. The two should go hand in hand-the obligation and the privilege.
The hon. gentleman says that war service should be the basis of war franchise; war service by whom? If he had said that war service in so far as the elector is concerned, should be the basis of war franchise, I would agree with him. But that is not the position which he takes. He does not say that the women of Canada who have worked faithfully during three or four years, day and night, knitting socks for the soldiers, collecting funds for the patriotic and red cross work, are entitled to the vote. No-; that is not service in the eyes of the Secretary of State. What he considers to be service is to stay at home, draw money from the Patriotic Fund, draw money from the Government, spend the separation allowance-and then vote; that is what he considers to be service. He bases the franchise of the woman, who remains at home on the service of the soldier who has gone across the ocean and is fighting on the other side for Canada and the Empire. He ignores the service which is rendered here at home. He ignores the service rendered by the wife of the munition worker-the man who for the past two or three years has been going day in. and day out to these munition plants, where the gases, which have practically ruined vegetation for miles around, have the same effect upon the human system as they have upon nature-he ignores the services of the wife who ministered daily to the wants of ' the husband as he came home from the munition plant, being well aware that he was dying a slow death for Canada and for the Empire. Yet this woman is to be deprived of the vote, and this man who is working in the munition factory will be deprived of the vote if he happens to be an alien who became naturalized in Canada within the last fifteen years.
The member for Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) brought up what he considered to be
a new phase of the question; he gave us a definition of the word "nationals." The Conservative party always have to be coupled up with some other organization. When it is not the nationals, it is the Nationalists; when it is not the Nationalists, it is the nationals. To-day they are coupling themselves up with the nationals. What, after all, is the definition of a national? A man who is naturalized here in Canada? A man who is the possessor of a Canadian naturalization certificate? No; a man who can be obliged to go and fight on the other side; a man who will perform active military service. If the Government wish to be consistent, why do they not disfranchise every man who is too old to fight? These aliens who have been in this country since 1902 have done their share in this war. They have contributed very generously in certain cities of Canada to Patriotic and Red Cross Funds and to the Belgian Relief Fund; those who have not contributed in that way have felt the pinch of the high cost of living due to the war. After paying directly and indirectly-for several years their share of taxation for the carrying on of the war,, they are told that they have not the-right to vote. The Government borrowed! . every dollar they could raise in Canada at five per cent; then they crossed tothe United States and paid six per cent to the Americans, to get money to pay the interest charges on the money which they had borrowed at home. The aliens in Canada of alien birth are helping to pay these charges: yet they are not to have the right to vote. Where is the good old British motto of "No taxation without representation?" These men are being taxed, yet they are to have no right to decide who shall govern this country. What about the statement concerning "the scrap of paper?" When we entered this war Liberals and Conservatives alike on recruiting platforms ir. the province of Quebec-and I dare say in every part of Canada-referred often tothe action of the German Government in-violating the neutrality of Belgium; of tearing up the treaty of years gone by, which was considered by them as a mere "scrap of paper." What about the promises made to these aliens who came into Canada in 1902-promises made by the Minister of the Interior in every administration, by the present leader of the Opposition when he was Prime Minister, by the present Prime Minister? According to the promises made, these people were to enjoy the privileges if.

"British subjects in Canada. The present leader of the Opposition has kept his word; ho is respecting his promise; he is voting and acting accordingly in the House of Commons. But because it suits the convenience of hon. gentlemen opposite to deprive these people of their votes; because they fear that they may vote for the Liberal party; because they fear that these people will consider that they can obtain more economic advantages in this country by voting for the Liberal party, the Government will deprive them of the vote. They might well have reflected: We have done so many things which were wrong; wc have spent the money of the people so ruthlessly since we have been in power, that we feel sure, even though we deprive these aliens of their votes, that we shall still not have enough votes to win the election; we will, therefore, give votes to the soldiers, not. only to the Canadian soldiers, but to those who never lived in Canada, never paid a cent of taxation in Canada, and do not know anything about the administration of this country. They are fighting for the Allies, the same as the British, French and American soldiers; but they happen to be enlisted in the Canadian army, and we will give them the right to vote; we will give them the right to put their votes where they want to put them, in whatever constituency they may choose; but we will take the vote from the alien who has paid taxes for years.
It is evident that the purpose of bringing down this legislation was not that of winning the war, but that of winning the forthcoming election. The proof of that is the statement which I have already referred to, that service should be the basis of war franchise, and that war service should be interpreted as relationship with the soldier who happens to be fighting for us on the ether side of the ocean. If that is the way service is to be measured, it is only fair to argue that the sister who happens to have two brothers fighting on the other side of the ocean should have two votes, because she is giving more service to the country than the sister who has only one.
Another conclusion would, perhaps, be that those who have given their sons in death to the Empire, whose sons have sacrificed their lives for their King and country, should have more votes than those whose relatives have come back with only one arm or with only one hand. That would be a logical conclusion, if we are going to accept the argument taken by the

Solicior General, who says that service is to be the basis. If service of the man overseas is to be the basis and not the service of the person at home, it would be just as logical to say that the minor children oi the soldiers should vote-I am frank to say that it will require the votes oi 1 a.m. the minor children to win this election for the Conservative party, and I am very much surprised that this provision has not been included in the Bill. The Government were anxious enough to include anything and everything. Why did they not include in the Bill a provision by which the minor children of our .soldiers could vote, and by which the Conservative local candidate would be appointed tutor to those minor children to see that they voted right? That would be about as reasonable as the Bill which is now before us. That is not all. People, if their names do not happen to be upon the list as made by the enumerator of the Conservative party, must take an oath that they have a right to vote. I am afraid the Solicitor General has made a mistake in drawing up the formula of the oath that appears in this Bill. He should have stipulated that a man, before he is given the right to vote, must solemnly swear and affirm that he will vote for the Conservative party. That has not been done. It should have been done; otherwise I fear the Conservative party, by introducing this measure, will be hurting the fair name of Canada by discouraging immigration for years after the war without doing any good to itself and certainly without doing any good to our common country.

The hour is late, but there are a few minutes left to us before the guillotine will fall and we shall be deprived of the liberty of further expressing our views on the second reading of this Bill. I desire to give notice that before the conclusion of my remarks, I shall move, seconded by Mr. Sinclair,
That the said Bill be not now read a second time, but that It be resolved that in the opinion of this House it is not desirable, as provided by the said Bill, to disfranchise large numbers of the people of Canada who have taken the oath of allegiance, have been guaranteed the rights of citizenship in the name of His Majesty the King, and who have not failed to discharge all the obligations of citizenship.
And further that It be resolved that any measure granting the franchise only to a limited number of women, as proposed by the Bill, is contrary to the public interest and fails to recognize the splendid patriotic work which has been performed by the women of Canada generally during the present war.

There are one or two matters with which I should like to deal, and more especially with the observation of my hon. friend the member for Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett), who put forward the extraordinary proposition that there was no obligation whatever upon the part of the Government, as representing His Majesty the King, either to confer or to continue the right of franchise upon British subjects who had become such by reason of their having been naturalized. I was surprised at that statement of my hon. friend. In support of it he quoted certain language of one of the Lord Justices of England, but I am quite sure that that language must have been used with reference to a statute of the province of British Columbia whose authority was then in question; because, so far as the Parliament of Canada is concerned, no one would ever question its legal authority to take away from any citizen of Canada the right to exercise his franchise. That is within the power of Parliament, just as a provincial legislature in the exercise of the exclusive power conferred upon it by the British North American Act can deprive a citizen of his property without any compensation. But that I would' say would be tyrannical, an arbitrary and an unjustifiable exercise of its power; no one would say that it was just or equitable for a provincial legislature, though it -may have the power to do so, to deprive a man of his property without compensation. Now all that we say here is that the Parliament of Canada passed a law under which it provided certain means by which an alien may become a British subject, and it provides that when the conditions of naturalization are all fulfilled, by residence, by the necessary affidavits, and by the action of the court after public notice, the alien who so becomes a British subject becomes entitled to all the .political and other rights, powers and privileges which belong to a natural-bom British subject. Those are the words of the statute. Section 24 of the Naturalization Act, Chapter 77 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, says:
An alien to whom a certificate of naturalization is granted shall, within Canada, be entitled to all political and other rights, powers and privileges, and be subject to all obligations to which a natural-born British subject is entitled or subject within Canada.
What words could be stronger or more emphatic? My hon. friend from Calgary seemed to distinguish in some way between political rights and the right of franchise. But Parliament does not limit the right of
[Mr. Pugsley.j
the naturalized British subject to political rights, but gives to him all the political rights, powers and privileges of a natural-born British subject. Now when these citizens of Canada became naturalized, they became British subjects within Canada with the same rights, powers and privileges, and subject to the same obligations, as natural-born British subjects. That is the privilege which the Canadian Government and the Canadian Parliament have held out to all people in all parts of the world. They have said through their legislation, if you come to Canada and qualify by reason	of residence,	and by theauthority of the 'Court- before which you appear	you become	a	naturalized
British subject, then in the future no distinction will be made between you and the man- who is a natural-born British subject. Surely, Mr. Speaker, when the certificate of naturalization was given to these citizens declaring that they should have under the Canadian statute all the political and -all the other rights, powers, and privileges which a natural-born British subject enjoys within Canada, that was a promise, a guarantee of the rights of citizenship, which ought not to be taken away so long as a naturalized citizen discharges the obligations which he assumed under section 24 of the statute, namely, that he should bear all the obligations borne by a natural-born British subject.
Now it is not pretended that these citizens whom it is proposed to disfranchise have not performed their obligations, but ;t is said that as they are exempted from military service, therefore it is in the interest of the State that the franchise should be taken away from them. That might be an argument if these men had come and asked this Parliament to exempt them from military service, but they have asked nothing of the kind.
No evidence has been submitted to this House of any desire on their part for military exemption, but this disfranchisement applies to every one of these naturalized military subjects who . are above military -age, and who are exempt from military service. Let me -ask yo-u, Sir, in the name of justice and fairplay, if, because you exempt from military service a young man between twenty and thirty-five, residing iin Canada, it is any justification to take away the franchise from thousands upon thousands of men of the same race who are upwards of the age of thirty-five who cannot be called upon under the Military Service Act to perform military duty. Where is the justification for it? Is it not all a

pretense when those gentlemen come before this House and say that is the ground upon which they put it? If that is the ground, why did they not limit the disfranchisement to those young men of alien enemy origin who are exempted specially by the statute from military service? Surely these men, who have reached the age of thirty-five years and are given the guarantee of all the rights, political and otherwise which appertain to the natural-born British subjects, are entitled to retain their franchise just the same as British-born subjects who have attained the .age of thirty-five, in neither case is there any liability for military service, both classes are by law British subjects, the one is a natural-born British subject the other is a naturalized British subject. They are both declared by law to have the same political Tights, powers, and privileges. And so I ask you upon what principle of justice shall one be treated differently from the other? I say it is all a pretense, and I shall tell you why I say so. There was an assurance-and I have every reason to believe it because I have it on very high authority- that if our western Liberal friends who were in favour of conscription would come in and help to form a union government this measure of disfranchisement would not be introduced. I have the proof in the procedure before this Parliament, and it is that there was no exemption of those naturalized British subjects [DOT] in 'the Military Service Act. They were to be liable to serve, just as the British-born were liable to serve, but when the union government fell through, after the piteous appeals which those gentlemen upon the other side were making to our Liberal friends in the West, confessing to them in effect that they had so lost the confidence of the people that they felt they could not successfully carry on the war, and urging and beseeching our Liberal friends in the West especially to join them in the formation of a union government, they come down with this disfranchisement Bill and put in this Bill relating to the franchise the extraordinary provision, which they omitted entirely from the Military Service Act, exempting those naturalized British subjects from military service. They put it in this Franchise Bill because the Military Service Act bad passed before the union government scheme had fallen through. Then they propose to disfranchise this large class of citizens, and in order to make it appear that there was some justification for 'it, they exempt a portion of these
men from military service. I am satisfied that the hon. gentleman sitting upon the treasury benches, and ithe hon. gentlemen behind them who have forced them in caucus to bring down this measure, have been justly charged with the fact that this Bill is to enable them to win an election. Some gentlemen of the Government say: "Well, suppose that is so; if it is we axe proud of it, if it is likely to enable us to win -an election." Well, a burglar may try to break in and steal, and he may he foiled in his purpose, and so gentlemen who would steal an election from the honesit voters of the country may be foiled in their purpose. The only offence charged against these people is that .the gentlemen who occupy the treasury benches think they are actuated by Liberal principles. Liberalism means liberty and freedom, and when the people realize the attempt which is being made -to commit ia great outrage upon -a most deserving portion of the population, I think they will resent it and punislh those who are the authors of such an infamous measure. In the election -the Italian navvy working on the railroad or working in the trenches will have a vote, but the men out on the western prairie, the naturalized British subjects, who -are affected by this Bill, who came to our western country nineteen years ago-because this Bill goes back that far-settling in the province of Saskatchewan, out upon the lonely prairie, in a district where there was no railroad, -no hamlet, a long distance fro-m all the comforts of civilization, those men who have -spent the best part of their lives there building up homes for themselves and their families, and who have taken -a splendid part in producing what is needed for 'the Empire during this war, are deprived of their vote. Those men who have real substance in the country, men who have been working to build up the country are -to have no right to -say how the country shall be governed during the next five years.
My hon. f-riends upon the other side try to make the country believe 'that this is but a war-time measure, only to last during the wiar. Have they * put in this Bill a clause that there shall be a dissolution of Parliament after the war is over? Not -much. If they are elected under this Bill, they will be able to hold office for five years after the election, and will be able to administer all the general affairs of the country, whether arising out of the war, or connected with the war, or otherwise.

Let me call your attention to the provision of the Bill referred to in this proposed amendment, the provision relating to women. The amendment I propose moving declares that any measure granting the franchise only to a limited number of women, as proposed in the Bill, is contrary to the publie interest and fails to recognize the splendid patriotic work which has been performed by the women engaged generally during the present war. I desire to express my entire agreement with hon. gentlemen upon this side of the House, as well as upon the other side, who have said it is eminently proper that the near relatives of those who have gone to the front should receive the franchise in the coming election. But, let us consider, for a moment, upon what it is based. It is not, .and cannot be, based upon the service which is given by men at the front. If it were, as my hon. friend from Shefford (Mr. Boivin) pointed out, the vote could not be given equally. I instance a case which comes within my own knowledge. A very dear friend of mine has three boys who have been at the front since the war broke out. These boys have only one sister, only one female relative. It would not be fair,, as the hon. member for Shefford has said, that there should be only one vote to represent those three boys. I know another case of one man who has gone to the front, and whose six or seven female relatives will have votes under this Act. Surely if the franchise was given on the theory that it is for the service of men at the front, that would he a very unequal representation, because in the one case there are .seven ladies voting representing one man, and in another one lady representing three men. Sir, it is based and must be based upon the service which the women themselves have Tendered to this country, based upon the sacrifices which they have made in parting from their sons, their husbands, their brothers. It must be based upon service, and it can be based upon notning else. Their service to the country has been great. Their sacrifice has been great, and every member will agree that it is manifestly proper that their services should be recognized and they should be given the vote. But while that is true, is it just that the women of the country who have performed such splendid service during this war should be deprived of the opportunity equally with the others of saying how this country shall be governed for the next five years? Upon what ground is it based? The women generally of this 
country have, as my proposed amendment states, performed splendid service. Will it be said that they have not shown that they are entitled to the franchise just as much as the men of this country are entitled to it? Can it be based upon the ground that the issues in the next election are simply to be issues connected with the war? I saw the other day that a prominent gentleman, in British Columbia took that ground. He referred to the Canadian Northern Railway Bill at a publie meeting, and said that in ordinary times the action of the Government in putting that Bill before Parliament would induce the people to say that they had brought ignominy and shame and disgrace upon this country; but, he said, because the war is on I must vote for them and support them. But that is not going to be the view the people of this country generally will take. They will say that the hoys at the front must be supported; that every possible effort should be made to win the war. But the question will be, who will take part in the governing of the country to enable the war to be won? Many questions will come up for the consideration of the electorate; some will take one side, others the other side. And let me say to my hon. friends, that they must not expect the people, the electors at large, will not desire to take all these questions into consideration. They will look, .and properly look, at the way in which this Government has managed the affairs of this country, both matters connected with the war and other matters of administration, during the years tlvey have been in power, and will determine whether or not it is in the best interests of thfe country to longer entrust the administration to their hands.
You say I have but one minute longer, Mr. Speaker? I shall avail myself of that one minute to say that I think it is a most reprehensible thing that, on a matter of such enormous importance as the disfranchising of thousands and thousands of the electors of this country, the conferring of the franchise upon a portion of the women of this country, we should have, on the very first day of the discussion upon the second reading of this Bill, the application of the closure, so that reasonable and fair opportunity for discussing this measure is refused. The question is so important that a very much larger time ought to be giveu to it. The people of this country are entitled to be informed. Hon. gentlemen think that because we cannot convince them we lhave no right to speak. I trust that, through the press, our voices will go beyond

be heard by the great court of the nation, toe court to which hon. gentlemen opposite and we must soon appeal and submit our case. And I ask, is it not contrary to all reason and fair play to the people of this country that a measure of this enormous importance should be pressed through by closure on the very day succeeding* t6e motion for the second reading, which is the first opportunity given in this Parliament for a full and fair discussion? Is it treating the people of this country fairly? I submit that it is not. This country is many thousand miles in extent. There are, 1 venture to say, thousands of people in Canada who have not yet heal'd of the contents of this Bill; men engaged upon the farms, men who receive their newspapers only weekly, men who have many other subjects to engage their attention. It takes days for thejn to learn what is going on in this Parliament, even to leam what is going on, to say nothing of getting particulars of the proposed legislation.
I will not trespass for one single instant upon the time of the House; but I desire to say that I do believe, and I think it will be the verdict of the people of this country, that never in the history of Cam ada has there been, and I trust that never again in the history of Canada will there be, a measure so unjust, a measure so objectionable in its character, a measure so incapable of defence from every reasonable standpoint, as the measure which is now before the House.

Rouville asked if I would see 'him next, and I have to do so.

This measure is certainly the most important that has come up before Parliament for many years, and, as my friend the member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) has just said, it means the disfranchising of thousands and thousands of Canadians, full-fledged British subjects. I only regret that we have to discuss this question at this late hour and under such circumstances. Some years ago, in reading an account of the sinking of the Titanic in mid-ocean, I was struck with the last words uttered by the captain of the ship, ffhose who were saved on that memorable night said that they heard the voice of the captain telling his crew: Be British. These were the last words uttered by that gallant captain, so the confines of this room and that we shall
faithful to the best traditions of Great Britain on the sea. Sir, it seems to me that the captain of the ship of state could give us to-day some words of the same nature. But as I see the Tory ship sinking on the eve of a general election, I am afraid that the voice of the captain is uttering other words than those of the gallant captain of the Titanic. He is telling his crew to be Prussians and to be Hunnish. This measure is most unjust, most unfair, and most ungenerous. A Bill such as this would delight the heart of any junker in Germany. It would be hailed with pleasure, with enthusiasm by General Caranza or, if he were living, by General Huerta, in Mexico.
We have been told this afternoon, in very-eloquent terms, the causes of the war in South Africa. The hon. gentleman from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) told us what. happened in the Boer republic when the franchise was refused to the British subjects. I had intended to quote from the first chapter of the book which had a great circulation at the time of the declaration of war against the Boer republic, entitled "The Transvaal from Within," by Sir Percy Fitzpatrick. I shall not quote from it, because my hon. friend gave us the causes of the war in South Africa and the reasons why men from all parts of the British Empire went to South Africa, in order to stand by the men of British birth who were refused their rights by the President of the Boer republic. Let me, however, quote the memorial signed by the president of the Reform Committee in the Transvaal Republic. The great grievance, indeed the most conspicuous grievance, of the British subject in the Transvaal was the refusal by the Boer Government of the franchise. The memorial says:
Our great effort, however, was the petition for the franchise with the moderate terms of which you are all acquainted. The petition was signed by more than 38,000 persons. What was the result? We were called unfaithful for not naturalizing ourselves when naturalization means only that we should give up our original citizenship and get nothing in return, and become subject to disabilities.
Further on the memorial says:
We have now only two questions to consider :-[DOT]
Says Mr. Leonard, chairman of the Transvaal National Union, summing up the grievances of the British subjects:
-(a) What do we want? (h) How shall we get it? X have stated plainly what our grievances are, and I shall answer with equal directness the question, ''What do we want?" We want:	The establishment of this republic as
a true republic; (2) a Grondwet or constitu-

tion which shall be framed by competent persons selected by representatives of the whole people and framed on lines laid down by them -a constitution which shall be safeguarded against hasty alteration; (3) an equitable franchise law, and fair representation; (4) equality of the Dutch and English languages.
Sir, in South Africa the British subjects,, being refused their franchise, revolted and called the Britons from all parts of the British Empire to come to their rescue, and they came to the rescue tor that very purpose. I remember the occasion when the resolution was presented to the House of Commons. I was then one of the budding members of that Chamber. I had been elected in 1896, and that resolution was presented by the then Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and seconded by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) in 1897. My hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) quoted from the speech delivered by the then Prime Minister of Canada the resolution which was adopted unanimously by the members of the House. But there is another speech which should arrest the attention of the hon. gentlemen vho sit at your right, Mr. Speaker, the members who belong, to the Orange lodges. I remember the speech delivered on, that occasion by one of the most eminent of the Orange leaders in Canada. I refer to the late Clarke Wallace, father of the present member for Centre York, who used the following language:
British subjects have been deprived of the rights of citizenship which Great Britain has given in every land where her flag has waved. We in Canada have given a conspicuous example of that because here the fullest measure of freedom and liberty has been given to those who are not British born. We may perhaps say that greater freedom has been given by Great Britain than by any other nation to those not native born, because we have been examples of the great liberality with the most successful and satisfactory results. I desire to add my, word of commendation to the resolution proposed by the right hon. leader of the Government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier).
Here is the language of a gentleman who, in his day and generation, was the most-eminent member of the Orange Order, and he stood in his place in Parliament and supported the leader of the Government and his friend the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster). He stood by them, because the franchise had been refused the British-born in South Africa by Paul Kruger. I wish that the men who belong to the Orange lodges would follow in the footsteps of the late Clarke Wallace, and remember the timely words he uttered on that historic occasion.

The present Government sitting to your right, Mr. Speaker, is only there on sufferance. The life of this Parliament has been extended, and I regret, Mr. Speaker, having assented to that extension. I was under the impression that that extension was granted last year to carry on the war, as was stated at the time, but what has happened? The Government, despite the pledges that were given by its members, forced through, first, a conscription measure, thus sowing the seed of disunion amongst a united people. The Government	has-how shall I say it-
Siftonized a deal of stupendous magnitude by this Canadian Northern transaction, adding six hundred millions toi the national debt of Canada. And now the Government comes at the end of this session with a Bill, not of enfranchisement, hut of disfranchisement, making of the most solemn pledges and of our naturalization laws so many "scraps of paper," so that, at the next general election, Hun-like, yes, Kaiser-like, they may hack their way through the constituencies of Canada. My hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) expressed 'surprise that closure had been used on this occasion. I am not surprised that closure has been adopted. The instrument is worthy of the occasion. This is class legislation, and reactionary legislation. The Tory Government is reverting to mediaeval times, when foreigners were only tolerated in so-called civilized countries, and were hardly recognized .as human beings.
We hear the suggestion at almost every turn:	cease to be Liberals; forget your
party ties and your party relations; be Canadians; >be British, so that we may win the war. Yet a most un-British, a most unCanadian measure is proposed by the Government, to serve, under the cover of patriotism, the most selfish party ends of the Tory party. This Bill emphasizes more than ever the essential and radical difference between Liberalism and Conservatism. Gladstone was a great reformer in the sense of extending the franchise; as a matter of fact, any one who has read the history of the Mother Country knows that the Reform Bills were introduced and passed by "Liberal governments as they were opposed by Tory oppositions.' The great Gladstone has given to the following definition of Liberalism and Conservatism :
The principle of Liberalism is trust in the people, qualified by prudence; the principle of Conservatism is mistrust of the people, qualified by fear.

I am prouder than ever of my Liberalism and of the guiding principle of my political faith; trust in the people. The present measure introduced by the Government shows exactly where the Tory party always stands. The Tory party stands for privileges, for class legislation, for mistrust of the people, qualified by fear of the electorate. The old conception of society was a conception of classes. Human beings in the old days-not so very old after all; in the beginning of the last century-were graded and standardized; certain privileges were reserved to certain groups. The first Reform Bill was introduced by an ancestor of one of the great Governor Generals, Lord Grey; others came later from G adstone and from leaders of Liberal and Radical governments. These Reform Bills were so many steps towards, equal rights.
* Sir, we have brought to Canada immigrants from all parts of the world. We have advertised Canada as the land of the free. We promised the immigrants equality of rights. They were living in Europe in their native lands in a state of serfdom; we gave them freedom as they came within our gates. The nationalities spread over the famous and historic Balkan peninsula have been living in serfdom, some under the yoke of Austria, others under the yoke of Turkey. Do you think that the men who lived in serfdom in those countries have any regard for the masters whom they left, for the yoke from which they were freed? As I read the other day a passage from a very interesting book on immigration, it dawned upon me that it was not possible that a Galician, for instance, although an Austrian subject, would have any regard for Austria; that on the contrary, having sworn allegiance to His Majesty the King and become a full-fledged British subject settled in the great far West, the possessor, indeed, the proprietor of 700 acres of land-would always side with Canada ano Britain in preference to Austria. Speaking of the Galician, Mr. Woodsworth, in his excellent book on immigration, "Strangers within our Gates," says:
He is ambitious. He is eager to become Canadianized. He does not cling to a language which is rich in words that express sorrow and despondency and misery, and meagre in those that express aspiration and joy and hope. Above all, he yearns to get on the land and to own some acres of his own. A Roman Catholic priest tells of conducting a Galician and, his wife to a quarter-section he had helped them to secure for homesteading. The man could hardly believe that the land on which he stood was, on certain conditions, to be actually his own.
